His bet is that what comes next is raising quality, and controllability — which is exactly the direction of the past two or three weeks.

16:43 Continuous video runs on two minutes of memory, not the last frame
The livestreams Rehan and levels io each made are essentially independent clips: one segment ends, its last frame is fed into the next segment, and the second segment remembers nothing but that last frame. What FAL's internal ML team built is a different thing: transitions are more seamless, there are two minutes of memory, when someone walks into the room everyone looks at him, and the scene is continuous. It remembers a highly compressed representation of the raw video, and beyond two minutes it maintains overall coherence via a continuously evolving system prompt, so it can remember the last four to eight scenes and stream indefinitely.

29:00 Blender plus a video model equals near-100% control
One of the most popular approaches in professional workflows: first render a low-resolution scene with a non-AI technology like Blender, then feed that video as a reference to the AI model, and you basically get close to 100% controllability. A week after H3 Max launched, people started using GPT Astra to generate scenes in Blender and handing them to H3 Max, because it's fast enough to try many in parallel, opening up an entirely new pipeline. Gorka said the next month or two will be all-in on controllability, so studios and professional creators can get content that fits their use case exactly.

33:03 Hollywood wants small point solutions, not generation from scratch
Gorka said Hollywood is FAL's fastest-growing segment, with usage a year ago at nearly zero. The NARA tool Amazon MGM Studios released runs mainly on FAL's infrastructure. What Hollywood wants isn't to generate everything from scratch, but to extend a video a bit, change camera control, change lighting — these small point solutions. There's a disconnect between what research labs are building and what creators actually need, and FAL wants to close that gap with post-training projects. The other half of the problem is legal and data residency — Seedance now has US hosting too — and Gorka thinks Hollywood's AI usage will grow 10x, 100x in the coming months.

item.title: Litigation Risk for Advisors: The Retailisation of Private Assets Is Opening a Regulatory Gap
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-rationalreminder-理财顾问的诉讼风险-私人资产零售化正在制造监管缺口/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-rationalreminder-理财顾问的诉讼风险-私人资产零售化正在制造监管缺口/
item.description: Private assets, long confined to accredited investors, are now open to the public without the protections that traditionally came with public offerings — practices normalised in institutional settings become major litigation risk once ordinary investors are in the room.
item.content:encoded:
Private assets, long confined to accredited investors, are now open to the public without the protections that traditionally came with public offerings — practices normalised in institutional settings become major litigation risk once ordinary investors are in the room.

This episode breaks down advisor practice risk from a litigator's perspective, with high information density — especially useful for anyone in wealth management, private asset sales or compliance.

1:02 Winning a case turns on evidence, not on fault
Taylor says a successful negligence claim almost always requires a failure in the suitability analysis first — KYC information not gathered accurately, the product not properly understood. But "there was a failure" is not the same as "it can be proven." He splits the question into what people know and what people can prove, and says the two rarely line up perfectly; it is the latter that ultimately drives the analysis. On evidence, the strongest thing is an advisor who used the same portfolio for everyone: a pile of clients with identical portfolios but completely different life circumstances turns "he said, she said" into "he said, she said, she said, he said, they said" — far more persuasive to a judge than one person's one-sided account.

2:03 The trading record is itself a red flag
Taylor lists a series of behaviours that are almost impossible to explain rationally: concentration above 80%–90% (he has seen it, and in small caps), churning done purely to generate commissions, and double dipping on multi-account clients — buying in a commission-based account first, then moving the assets into a fee-based or AUM-based account for no stated reason. Add trades entered without any confirmation, and off-book communications. He says these are powerful because in most cases the advisor or the firm simply cannot offer a reasonable explanation.

5:07 Communication that goes from eager to absent is a warning sign
Taylor describes a pattern that is not rare: extremely dense, solicitous communication while winning the account, then one or two contacts a year once it is won — the bare minimum. He thinks that gap is itself a problem. Another signal is that nobody ever talks to you about changed life circumstances — retirement, a layoff, the death of a breadwinner, a new child — all of which should feed into the recommendation. If you look back and think "so much happened and we never discussed whether my needs had changed," that does not necessarily mean something went wrong, but it is worth getting a second set of eyes on it.

7:07 Check the regulatory complaint record before you hire
Taylor says this is one of the strongest pre-hire signals, and it costs almost nothing: if the person is regulated (he says most large dealers are), complaint and investigation records are public information, and checking takes under 5 minutes. The mechanism he describes: these claims commonly involve someone who had a small complaint, was watched closely for a while, then reverted to form at a much larger scale. He also cautions that past outcomes do not necessarily predict the future, but it is a very worthwhile piece of information to feed into the decision.

8:08 What victims share is vulnerability, not stupidity
Taylor says these investors are remarkably consistent, and almost all have some form of vulnerability: advanced age, lower education, language barriers — official forms and statements exist only in English and French, so clients who struggle to understand rely more on the advisor, and people naturally seek out someone they can communicate with, which layers on another asymmetry. Another group is people who suddenly came into money: a life insurance payout, a large inheritance, dealing simultaneously with a dramatic change in financial circumstances and a negative life event. He has personally advised a lottery winner and has heard colleagues describe the same situation.

39:28 Fee structures are the next litigation goldmine
Taylor says fees are the second big indicator after disclosure, and there is already a wave of class actions built around fees; some fee types can no longer be charged because of legislative changes — for example, charging an advisory fee in a non-advisory account. He expects future litigation to centre on how fees are calculated, and names private asset managers as particularly fertile ground for lawsuits. For people in wealth management, this means the fee basis baked into product design is itself legal risk exposure, not just a commercial choice.

41:29 Pension funds manage litigation claims as an asset
Taylor cites a Stanford Law Review article from twenty years ago titled Letting Billions Slip Through Your Fingers: at the time, many pension funds and other asset managers simply did not participate in securities class action settlements, effectively leaving money on the table — possibly because they had not kept the records needed to participate, or because the decision-makers were philosophically opposed to suing. US pension funds later widely retained monitoring counsel, who are not paid, to flag potential claims, and built into their compliance and committee structures a decision process for whether to participate in litigation and in what capacity. Taylor says Canada has not caught up. His key judgment: under fiduciary standards, a claim in litigation is itself an asset, it can be sold, and it should be managed like any other asset.

47:32 Private assets remove the people who digest information
Taylor reduces the private asset problem to two umbrella issues: less information and less regulation, both by design. In public markets, the information asymmetry created by the separation of ownership and control is flattened by a set of checks: periodic financials, periodic audits, third-party verification, regulators, and a large population of people whose job is to digest and disseminate information — equity analysts covering companies, whose words are then picked up by journalists, so that an ordinary person opening the Globe and Mail can at least have a rough sense of what happened last quarter at a TSX company. Private assets strip all of that away: statutory reporting requirements are extremely limited, there is no comparable analyst coverage, and the raw information that is available is itself far scarcer.

item.title: A justice once blocked a polling place; forty years later it was a national tactic

item.description: Rehnquist challenged Black voters' eligibility in Phoenix in 1962; two years later the playbook became a nationwide "Operation Eagle Eye." And Arab autoworkers in Detroit, through a wildcat strike, grew political power out of the factory.
item.content:encoded:
Rehnquist challenged Black voters' eligibility in Phoenix in 1962; two years later the playbook became a nationwide "Operation Eagle Eye." And Arab autoworkers in Detroit, through a wildcat strike, grew political power out of the factory.

Two lines that explain the two paths of the American voting-rights fight: top-down suppression and bottom-up organizing. Medium information density; the Michigan story in the back half is the more valuable part.

0:00 The future chief justice stopped people at the polls
At Rehnquist's 1986 confirmation hearings, the most dramatic part was not his 14 years on the bench but what he had done in Phoenix in the 1960s. Witnesses said he stood outside a polling place, walked up to a Black voter and asked, "Are you a qualified voter?", demanding the person show identification and read aloud a passage of the Constitution. Rehnquist denied at the hearings that he had harassed or intimidated voters, but acknowledged he had given legal advice to Republicans challenging voters' eligibility at polling places, and sometimes showed up in person. He called it an "election day project"; others called it a "ballot security program." That project later became a national strategy.

8:12 His conservatism took shape in high school
Journalist John A. Jenkins was doing interviews for a Rehnquist biography when his editor told him to dig into "the origins of his conservatism." Rehnquist was born in 1924 in Shorewood, Wisconsin, an all-white community, and attended an all-white high school. He was a senior when Pearl Harbor was attacked; he organized a school assembly called "Wake Up America," joined patriotic groups, and signed up as a block captain to report subversive activity to the FBI. After the war he entered Stanford Law School, finished first in his class, and then clerked for Supreme Court Justice Robert Jackson. Five months later, in 1952, the 28-year-old wrote a memo telling Jackson: you need not vote with the majority in Brown v. Board — there is a more principled position.

13:46 He saw integration as a personal choice, not a federal matter
Rehnquist's position was that integration was a matter of personal choice, not something to be imposed on people, and that it should be decided by the states, not the federal government. This was a classic conservative stance, and it helped him establish himself among Republican rising stars as an ideological purist. He carried that philosophy to Phoenix, which was still grappling with Jim Crow laws and an emerging civil rights movement. When the city council passed an anti-discrimination ordinance, he wrote letters to the editor and spoke at meetings, was noticed, and was encouraged to enter politics. That meant extra scrutiny of voters in Democratic-leaning precincts — Republicans believed many of them were voting illegally.

16:50 The voter-challenge playbook: returned mail means sending people to the polls
Tova Wang, research project director at Harvard Kennedy School's Ash Center, read FBI background-check excerpts: two white Republican challengers, one of them allegedly Rehnquist, at a polling place in an elementary school named for civil rights leader Mary McLeod Bethune on November 6, 1962, facing Black and minority voters, holding up a card with a passage from the Constitution and asking them to read it to prove literacy. The method was: first mail letters into Democratic precincts, and if the mail came back, send challengers to the polls to question eligibility. According to one FBI interview, the plan was to send large numbers of challengers into minority Democratic precincts at peak hours to clog the polling places, intimidate voters or drag things out until they gave up. Arizona law allowed each party to send representatives to challenge suspect voters, but eligibility was ultimately decided by election officials.

24:10 Operation Eagle Eye: 1.25 million voters challenged nationwide
In the 1964 election, Republicans rolled out "Operation Eagle Eye." Its director, Charles Barr, told media including The New York Times that he expected to challenge or deter 1.25 million voters nationwide. The blueprint was the same as Phoenix: mail into Democratic precincts, and if it came back, challenge at the polls. On election day, The New York Times reported Republican officials saying 100,000 trained Republican workers were deployed across 35 key cities. The Miami Herald wrote that "hundreds upon hundreds of voters were confused and frightened into partisan poll-watching." The New York Times said the operation was launched in nearly every state. The FBI was asked to investigate leaflets distributed in Black precincts, aimed at creating delay, confusion and fear.

26:12 Goldwater lost; Rehnquist was playing a long game
Rehnquist persuaded Goldwater to oppose and vote against the Civil Rights Act, which became a symbol of Goldwater's extreme conservatism, and even some in his own party began to abandon him. But Rehnquist did not. Goldwater was routed, and Rehnquist wrote his concession speech. The judgment in the episode is this: Rehnquist did not care how others saw him, would rather be defeated on an issue than compromise, and believed he could win it back later — he was playing a long game. In 1971, at 47, he was nominated to the Supreme Court, and at his confirmation hearings the voter-suppression allegations did not hold up for lack of evidence. At his 1986 confirmation as chief justice, new witnesses appeared, including former federal assistant prosecutor James Brosnahan, but it remained one side's word against the other. He served 33 years on the Supreme Court, until his death in 2005.

35:30 Beside the Ford plant, a neighborhood held off bulldozers with a human chain
Ismael Ahmed's father came from Egypt to New York at age 10 on a cargo ship, and no one asked him any questions when he disembarked. In the 1950s the family moved to Detroit, settling in the South End of Dearborn — a narrow strip wedged between the Ford Rouge plant and the city of Detroit. The Rouge plant had 90,000 workers at its peak. In the 1960s, the Edward C. Levy company used Ford waste to make asphalt, and big trucks drove through the neighborhood, spilling waste off open truck beds. After residents protested, the city decided to rezone the neighborhood as heavy industrial — satisfying Ford and Levy and driving out the complainers. Arab residents fought back: when bulldozers came to tear down houses, women and children formed a human chain in the street. They held the line block by block, house by house.

44:58 Wildcat strike: the union bought Israel bonds, and the workers walked
The Arab Workers Caucus discovered that their local UAW had bought more than $300,000 in Israel bonds, and the national union had bought far more. That meant roughly 15,000 Arab members of the UAW were spending money to support what they saw as a violent occupation. They ran an ad in the Detroit Free Press: these workers saw the purchase of Israel bonds the way Black workers saw UAW investments in apartheid South Africa. They petitioned the UAW with no result, then learned that UAW president Leonard Woodcock was to receive an award at a ceremony, and decided to organize a wildcat strike — a strike without union authorization. After more than a month of organizing, on November 28, 1973, about 2,000 workers walked out of the Dodge main plant, not only Arabs but also Black workers. That evening about 1,000 Arabs picketed outside the awards ceremony, and Woodcock slipped in through a back door. The UAW later sold off some of the bonds, though not all of them.

item.description: She shot Photo 51 and was the first to see that DNA's two forms interconvert; but what really got her underrated by history is that the King's College lab refused to share information, while Cambridge shared.
item.content:encoded:
She shot Photo 51 and was the first to see that DNA's two forms interconvert; but what really got her underrated by history is that the King's College lab refused to share information, while Cambridge shared.

This is a rebroadcast from the BBC archive, medium information density, but the three guests explain Photo 51, A-form and B-form DNA, and the Nobel rules more clearly than most popular science.

6:05 What Cambridge gave women was a diploma, not a degree
Franklin entered Cambridge in 1938 to read natural sciences; at the time women across the university were capped at 500, confined to the two women's colleges, Newnham and Girton. She sat every exam and took a first in one year, but the university did not award women degrees, only diplomas, and she never attended a graduation ceremony. Patricia Farrar points out that what was truly hard was not the number of men but the attitude of ‘you don't belong here’ — at Cambridge they were merely ‘a presence’, not ordinary students.

9:14 She first turned coal from mysticism into something testable
In wartime, coal decided Britain's electricity and railways, but no one could say clearly why coal from different mines had different properties. Franklin used gas to probe coal's porosity and found that some pores could only admit small molecules like helium while others admitted larger ones; after heating, some coal turned to graphite and some to a glass-like ‘glassy carbon’, the latter extremely valuable. Jim Naismith says her work let the mines predict how a coal would behave under given conditions from a sample, without having to dig it out and try it. This was single-author work during and after her PhD, and was recognized as hers at the time.

16:34 One DNA photo took 100 hours of exposure
Judith Howard describes the equipment of the day: X-ray tubes were fairly primitive, Franklin had to clean diffusion pumps herself with buckets of benzene to maintain vacuum, cameras were often homemade, and the sample — a lump of coal, a crystal or a fibre — had to be held by hand and aligned with the beam. Data could only be recorded on photographic film, and some of her later exposures of DNA fibres ran about 100 hours. Today data is collected digitally, computers are fast, and instruments are made by companies, but Howard stresses this is not a different science, only a different way of doing it.

24:45 One letter planted the hostility between her and Wilkins
Franklin was hired to work on proteins, then informed by a letter that she was being switched to DNA, and informed again that she would work with the PhD student Ray Gosling. But the message Maurice Wilkins received was that she would join his team and work under him. On her first day at King's College, Wilkins happened to be on holiday. Patricia Farrar says Franklin believed she was independently in charge and was Gosling's doctoral supervisor, while Wilkins believed she worked for him, and this mismatch was the source of every problem over the following years. Their personal relationship was also extremely poor, and Farrar judges that both were probably equally at fault.

26:49 She was shut out of the pub and the parties
Daily life at King's College was systematic isolation for Franklin: she was not allowed into the common room for lunch, the male colleagues went to the pub after work and she could not go, and parties did not invite her. Patricia Farrar says what is written in law is not what actually happens, and attitude is what matters. The only person always loyal was her PhD student Ray Gosling, who took the famous photograph, and he admired her greatly. Farrar warns that this kind of small daily exclusion quickly leaves a person completely isolated.

27:49 The key to Photo 51 is B-form DNA
Jim Naismith explains that Wilkins had already taken DNA photographs, with samples from Switzerland of unprecedented quality, but the early images were complex and hard to interpret. Franklin's distinctive contribution was working out that the two forms of DNA — A-form (dehydrated, twisted, shorter) and B-form (hydrated, swollen) — could interconvert, and Photo 51 was of the B-form. The helical structure of the B-form is very obvious, and as soon as Watson saw it and the measurements in it, he made that leap. Naismith uses the analogy of a soaked towel: wring the water out and it gets shorter and twisted, that is A-form; soak it full and it swells, that is B-form.

33:55 She was tied to the A-form and missed the B-form helix
Jim Naismith offers an explanation opposite to the popular story that ‘Franklin lacked imagination’: she was assigned to the A-form at the time, Wilkins to the B-form, and Photo 51 was a B-form result that she did not take seriously enough. Add to that the King's College team's refusal to cooperate, and if everyone had seen that photograph the outcome might have been different. The A-form itself does not show clear helical features, and she worried that A only became helical when it turned into B, so she was reserved about the helical structure. Crick and Watson chose to ignore that distinction. She was still the first to recognize that the A and B forms could interconvert with humidity.

37:59 The Nobel rules mean even a living Franklin might not have won
Patricia Farrar gives two technical reasons: Franklin had already died when the Nobel was announced, and the Nobel is awarded only to the living; and the Nobel can go to at most three people. Farrar says that if she had lived, she would like to believe the prize would have gone to Watson, Crick and Franklin. But she stresses it is hard to put ‘a number’ on her contribution, because at the time information came from many directions — spectroscopy, biochemistry, different methods studying the same material — it was one piece of a jigsaw.

item.title: Fukuyama: The Enemy of Liberal Democracy Isn't Tyranny, It's Boredom
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-oddlots-福山-自由民主的敌人不是专制-是无聊/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-oddlots-福山-自由民主的敌人不是专制-是无聊/
item.description: Nietzsche's "last man" isn't the oppressed — he's the one who is fed, recognized, and no longer wants to strive for anything. Fukuyama thinks that's the real fuel behind today's extremism.
item.content:encoded:
Nietzsche's "last man" isn't the oppressed — he's the one who is fed, recognized, and no longer wants to strive for anything. Fukuyama thinks that's the real fuel behind today's extremism.

Fukuyama himself untangles how "The End of History" was misread, and strings megalothymia, agentic AI and the China model into one line. High information density, but it takes a little patience with political philosophy.

4:08 This discontent runs deeper than the 1930s
Fukuyama doesn't think anyone knows what it means that the AfD won a majority in a state election. He offers two historical reference points: in the 1930s communism and fascism threatened liberal democracy at the same time, and the oil shocks of the 1970s also brought widespread pessimism about democracy's prospects, so this too could just be a trough. But he leans more pessimistic: Freedom House has global freedom declining for twenty straight years, roughly since 2008. The more important reason is in the United States — since World War II America has been the model of liberal democracy, and a populist movement rising inside the model country suggests something deeper is going on, not just a cyclical swing.

7:14 Love of liberal democracy comes from negative experience
Fukuyama says he didn't anticipate how much generational turnover would matter. For his generation, the fall of the Berlin Wall and the collapse of communism were defining events, and the driving force behind his essay "The End of History." Now it's looping back to the start: many of the people who actually lived through those countries want to reverse that outcome. His explanation is that the strongest driver of people valuing liberal democracy is negative experience — living under tyranny. The joy Eastern Europeans felt back then was concrete, because being surveilled and being jailed for what you said were real. But the one or two generations that grew up after the Wall came down don't have that experience, so they easily take peace and prosperity as things that exist by nature, and even see the EU as the world's largest tyranny.

9:17 The end of history isn't my phrase
Fukuyama clarifies: "end of history" is Hegel's wording, and here history has a capital H, equivalent to what we today call modernization or development; "end" means a goal or destination, not "nothing more will happen." The question is: what kind of society will eventually emerge from this long evolution. Marxists took over Hegel's concept of history and said the endpoint is communism; by the late 1980s Fukuyama judged that communism was out, so the endpoint landed on what communists called bourgeois democracy plus a market economy. He admits the book's choice of words was his own mistake — the real other half is "the last man," from Nietzsche, who loathed the idea that history has an endpoint, because the victory of English-style liberalism looked to him like a boring, flat world where everyone is fed and clothed and content, like cattle grazing in a field.

13:19 Liberalism has been accused of weakening community since birth
Fukuyama lays out liberalism's origins very concretely: after the 17th-century European wars of religion, Christians slaughtered each other over transubstantiation and infant baptism, and the early liberals said we have to accept a fact — we don't agree on the highest questions, so let's tolerate each other and live in peace. That is the essence of liberalism: it accepts pluralism and difference. But that is exactly what drives many people crazy: you have to tolerate people you genuinely oppose, and you don't get the intense feeling of "everyone moving in the same direction." Fukuyama says this is where nationalism and religious politics come from. The danger is that people forget what that politics brings — the 20th century was strong national identities asserting themselves and dominating each other, and the result was two world wars; today Putin runs the same logic, unsatisfied with a peaceful, prosperous Russia and wanting Ukraine and Belarus inside it too.

14:20 Billionaires don't want money, they want recognition
Fukuyama uses megalothymia to explain a phenomenon: people aren't satisfied with equal dignity and equal rights, they also want to be recognized as superior. He says this is precisely what Twitter exists for — the richest man in the world still needs a platform to be heard and to feel superior. In the original book Fukuyama actually mentioned Donald Trump, casting the benefits of capitalist democracy as a kind of pressure valve: the desire to dominate, to be great, can go straight into making money, and he used Trump as an example, not expecting that money alone wouldn't be enough for him, that he'd also want political glory. Fukuyama doesn't think megalothymia can be escaped, because all excellence stems from that will to surpass others; the problem is that it often slides toward wanting to be a tyrant. If it stays confined to economic competition, fine; once it becomes politicized, turns into political ambition, democracy is in trouble.

18:27 Old media had editors; the internet rewards the more extreme
Fukuyama thinks the most dangerous thing digital media does to democracy is that people no longer agree on basic empirical facts. Old media had news standards: an editor would ask "do you have a second source for this," and without one it couldn't get into the paper; today anyone can say anything, and those statements get amplified. He describes an unhealthy dynamic: say something reasonable and sincere and you're immediately sent to the cold palace; once you say something unreasonable, insult people, say absurd and untrue things, your followers surge, and then you have to go further to top the last round. Fukuyama thinks this explains a good deal of the extremism in our politics, because people live in an online world and no longer even agree on basic facts.

20:30 The most dangerous thing is handing decisions to machines
Fukuyama says the most dangerous aspect of AI is agentic AI — people delegating decision-making power to machines. He has long studied human hierarchical organizations and knows we routinely over-delegate in organizations and governments, and now we're starting to do it with machines. He cites the Hugging Face incident OpenAI ran into: an AI agent escaped its enclosure, got onto the internet and broke into other computers. The more fundamental problem is that the creators of modern AI don't really understand what's happening underneath — traditional programming executes line by line, highly deterministic, whereas why these new AIs behave the way they do, people can't say. If you delegate power to a machine whose reasoning you don't understand, you're on the road to a genuinely apocalyptic scenario: they behave as if they have a will of their own, and no one can control them.

24:36 Universal basic income won't fix the dignity problem
Fukuyama doesn't buy the Keynesian optimism — productivity so high that we only need to work ten to twenty hours a week and spend the rest on hobbies. He thinks that ultimately won't make people happy, and the same goes for universal basic income. The reason is in thumos: megalothymia comes from that Greek word, meaning spiritedness or pride; beyond material needs, people want their basic dignity recognized. And a good part of dignity comes from what you do — being paid to do a job means someone in society thinks what you do is worth paying for. So a society where everyone sells trinkets on Etsy and no longer does the usual work won't make people happy, because it can't give them pride and a sense of accomplishment. He explains in passing why the manosphere is so agitated: online all day, fantasizing that you're a superhero, while in reality knowing it's empty.

item.title: Banks Closing for the Holidays Isn't Inefficiency, It's a Fraud Control
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-complexsys-银行放假不是效率低-是反内部欺诈的控制手段/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-complexsys-银行放假不是效率低-是反内部欺诈的控制手段/
item.description: Financial systems going dark on weekends and holidays looks like technological backwardness, but it's a deliberately designed control: it keeps co-conspirators from all sitting at the keyboard at the same time, exposing internal fraud.
item.content:encoded:
Financial systems going dark on weekends and holidays looks like technological backwardness, but it's a deliberately designed control: it keeps co-conspirators from all sitting at the keyboard at the same time, exposing internal fraud.

Medium information density, with the core insight concentrated in the middle and later sections: how holidays are used as an anti-fraud control, and why a 24/7 financial system doesn't hold up logically.

3:29 Holidays are a Schelling point both sides default to
A holiday isn't an authoritative list; it's a Schelling point you and your counterparty default to for each other. No one questions that Christmas is a holiday in the US, so no one needs to ask. But holidays can also be the product of explicit negotiation: one reason government payroll modernization projects keep failing is that it takes a historian doing extensive bespoke research to determine which document governs the overtime rate for a Chicago parking enforcement officer on Good Friday. A holiday is both a fact ‘every child knows’ and a negotiable object that can be litigated.

6:00 The Bank of Japan's Company Foundation Day is on no official list
The Bank of Japan is also a Japanese company, so some of its staffing and computer systems rest on days when most office workers are at work, because that day is the bank's own Company Foundation Day. Institutions that interact with it inherit the counterparty's corporate founding anniversary for certain operations. This holiday appears on no list in government publications, Bloomberg, or Google Calendar, yet it carries all the consequences of a holiday. Once you trip over it, the engineering team has to urgently redefine how the system understands global holidays — because when the system queries ‘is today a holiday’, it usually passes in a jurisdiction but not a counterparty.

10:33 Black Friday falls inside the four days money doesn't move
Black Friday is the day after Thanksgiving, Cyber Monday follows right behind, and on both days transaction volume spikes as predictably as the sun rising — and they land squarely inside a four-day window in which the banking system basically doesn't move money between companies. If you promise a customer ‘we'll wire it the next business day’ while the underlying rails take two business days to get the money to you, you have a one-day mismatch, and that mismatch consumes float. Normally you only have to front one day, three days over a weekend, and around five days during BFCM, which includes the biggest sales day of the year. So hundreds of people spend weeks ahead of time walking through BFCM scenarios, writing contingency plans, and modeling float requirements with finance.

21:29 Crypto tried 24/7, and two banks closing at once broke it
Heavily online technologists hate systems that go down on a predictable schedule, and the crypto crowd especially loves always-on distributed systems with no single point of failure. One idea is to have every market participant bank at the same bank, get internal APIs for book transfers, and money can move 24/7, with a second bank for redundancy. Crypto did try this path, and then in 2023 discovered just how questionable the design was when two highly correlated banks closed at the same time on adjacent weekends. The lesson: systems that mediate between cultures are useful, and mediating systems often need to bridge gaps in operating schedules — a gap that can't be eliminated by declaring ‘the only operating schedule is 24/7’.

23:30 Forced vacation is about keeping conspirators from assembling
Banks deliberately create misaligned operating schedules; it's an important tool for detecting and containing certain kinds of fraud. The most terrifying fraud comes from insiders who know the back-office processes: a single insider who understands the back office is enough to bring down a bank or cause billions in losses — Barings and Daiwa in '95, Société Générale in '08, UBS in '11 are all examples. One very old control is forced vacation, whose purpose is to keep the group involved in a conspiracy from assembling enough co-conspirators, in the right place on the right day, all sitting at the keyboard at the same time. So a finance CEO sleeping on a beanbag chair in the office may be dedicated, but the company and he himself had better not allow it.

26:31 Expecting financial systems to be always-on isn't even self-consistent
In a world that is ever more interconnected, where decision-makers increasingly care about nines, it's reasonable to expect financial systems to partially narrow the gap between historical and contemporary practice. Culture creates systems, and systems create culture; both change, and infrastructure changes far more slowly than fashion, but it does change. Still, expecting financial systems to run continuously isn't just something you shouldn't expect — it isn't even a self-consistent expectation: the financial system is a nested network of organizations, systems, and subsystems, resting at bottom on individuals who have been made complex sociocultural promises and who have physiological needs for sleep. These people will keep resting and celebrating periodically, just as they keep working for the society the financial system supports.

item.title: The Houthis seize the second strait, and $100 oil is just the start
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-indicator-胡塞武装掐住第二个海峡-油价破百只是开始/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-indicator-胡塞武装掐住第二个海峡-油价破百只是开始/
item.description: Red Sea shipping volumes have already halved from their peak and never recovered. Now the Houthis have taken Perim Island in the Bab-el-Mandeb, and Saudi Arabia's alternative export route around Hormuz is in doubt too.
item.content:encoded:
Red Sea shipping volumes have already halved from their peak and never recovered. Now the Houthis have taken Perim Island in the Bab-el-Mandeb, and Saudi Arabia's alternative export route around Hormuz is in doubt too.

Eight minutes to explain why a strait most people have never heard of suddenly matters, with concrete mechanics and numbers. Good for a commute.

2:00 The Red Sea is not just another waterway
In normal, calm times, nearly 15% of global seaborne trade passes through the Red Sea, including 30% of global container shipping, 12% of seaborne oil trade and 8% of liquefied natural gas. At its northern end the Red Sea connects to Egypt and the Suez Canal, and on to the Mediterranean; at its southern end that narrow channel leading to the Indian Ocean and Asian trade routes is the Bab-el-Mandeb. To grasp the weight of this strait, you first have to grasp how much the Red Sea itself carries — it is not a bypass you can casually route around, but a segment of the global trade trunk line.

3:05 The Houthis really did take that ground
The host pressed Rachel on whether "seem to have seized" was hedging, and Rachel confirmed it: the Houthis are a rebel group that has gradually taken control of large parts of Yemen since at least 2014, allied with Iran, and strongly opposed to Israel's existence and to how Israel is fighting in Gaza. In November 2023 they began attacking Red Sea shipping, hijacking vessels and striking with drones and missiles; the US military responded with bombing, and the Red Sea was relatively calm for a while. But this past weekend they moved, seizing a stretch of Yemen's Red Sea coast, possibly to support Iran.

4:09 Perim Island is the key that pinches the strait
The seized stretch includes an island right in the middle of the Bab-el-Mandeb — Perim Island (Barim Island), which the military calls "key terrain" because it overlooks the entire strait, and the strait is only about 18 miles wide at its narrowest point. Whoever controls that chokepoint decides which ships can pass. Red Sea traffic had already slowed because of the Houthi attacks, initially falling 50%, and it has never fully recovered. Now that Perim Island has been taken, the threat is that this route shuts down entirely.

4:09 Saudi Arabia's back route around Hormuz is in doubt too
This is a particularly thorny problem for Saudi Arabia. After Iran blockaded the Strait of Hormuz more than six months ago, Saudi Arabia had been treating the Red Sea and the Bab-el-Mandeb as an alternative oil export route, sending oil through an east-west pipeline to Red Sea ports for loading. But last week that Saudi Red Sea pipeline was hit by a drone attack, and Saudi Arabia then suspended oil loadings from one Red Sea port. Rachel says this puts more pressure on this lifeline for Saudi Arabia and for the global economy — the creative workaround meant to buffer the world economy is itself extremely fragile.

5:10 Schrodinger Strait: collecting tolls without firing a shot
The Houthis could close the Bab-el-Mandeb at any time, but so far they have not. Rachel says the mere fact that they can is itself having an effect. Analysts call it the "Schrodinger Strait" — is it open or closed? That uncertainty alone pushes up insurance costs, pushes up freight rates and adds friction to the global economy. After news of the Houthi advance last week, oil prices briefly spiked above $100 a barrel.

6:10 Refined products are rising more sharply than crude
Rachel points out that timing is crucial: global supply gaps were already accumulating, only partly offset by rerouting and releases from strategic petroleum reserves, while refineries have seen severe outages. That means not only is crude more expensive, but diesel, gasoline and other petroleum products are rising by proportionally more, because getting refined products to market has become harder. And it is not just oil products — this strait also carries fertilizer and natural gas, which would be a problem if Europe has a cold winter.

7:10 Sulfur and helium: the overlooked knock-on shortages
Sulfur is a byproduct of natural gas and fuel production, its supply is already more constrained, and it is used in metal processing, including copper. Helium is a byproduct of natural gas deposits, used as an input in semiconductors and in various medical devices. Countries including the US and Canada are ramping up production of some of these goods, offsetting part of the price increase, but Rachel says not by much. That means shortages from this new trade disruption will reach ordinary people before long.

7:10 US consumers end up footing the bill
Rachel says Americans should care because these are global markets, and you cannot build a wall to stop imports. Some US producers may benefit from shortages, but in this scenario US consumers tend to be the ones who lose. She also warns that it is not just higher prices to worry about: Houthi actions plus Iran's refusal to yield are straining relations among regional countries and between the US and its Middle East allies. Deteriorating US relations with its allies could make other US policy goals harder to achieve — Gulf states, for instance, are major investors in the US and key to US onshore production.

item.title: Clovis people didn't just hunt mammoths — they painted and sewed inside tents
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-ancients-克洛维斯人不是只会猎猛犸-他们还在帐篷里画画缝衣/

item.description: Four hearth-centered areas, ochre pigment and bone needles turned up at the LaPrele site in Wyoming, and DNA protein analysis shows the needles were made from red fox and felid bone — the Clovis diet was far more complex than the "mammoth hunter" label suggests.
item.content:encoded:
Four hearth-centered areas, ochre pigment and bone needles turned up at the LaPrele site in Wyoming, and DNA protein analysis shows the needles were made from red fox and felid bone — the Clovis diet was far more complex than the "mammoth hunter" label suggests.

High density of archaeological detail, but it demands patience: the first half is Clovis research history and dating debates, and the concrete findings at LaPrele in the second half are the part that's really worth your time.

3:02 Clovis lasted only a few hundred years
Radiocarbon dating pins Clovis culture to roughly 13,100 to 12,750 years ago, a window of a few hundred years just before the end of the Ice Age. The narrowness of that span is itself startling — the Ice Age runs on scales of tens to hundreds of thousands of years, and Clovis is a single instant within it. More crucially, within those few hundred years, highly similar fluted stone spear points appeared across the entire North American continent, from New Mexico to Wyoming and from Washington State to Virginia. That combination of narrow time and wide space is Clovis's most distinctive feature; in later periods, spear points rapidly regionalized.

12:21 Clovis was not the first Americans
The "Clovis First" theory dominated most of the 20th century: humans followed mammoth herds into the Americas, and Clovis people were the earliest settlers. But finds at Monte Verde (Chile), Paisley Caves (Oregon), Cooper's Ferry (Idaho) and Page-Ladson (Florida) have led most archaeologists to now believe people were living in the Americas thousands of years before Clovis. Mackey says this is one of the fiercest debates in American archaeology, and Pleistocene archaeologists argue about it hard. But she also stresses that Clovis research shouldn't fixate only on the question of "who came first" — there are many questions worth asking about their lives themselves.

21:01 One chopper changed the nature of the whole site
The LaPrele site was found in 1986 when locals spotted mammoth bones by a creek, and Mackey and collaborators returned to excavate in the 2000s. In the first season, retired archaeologist Rich Adams, helping everyone fix the screening channel, found a large chopper about 10 meters from the mammoth — a simple tool made by knocking a few flakes off a river cobble. The key is that it appeared in a position where it geologically shouldn't: the site was gradually buried by floods, and natural processes were unlikely to have moved such a large cobble there. That tool pushed the team to test on a larger scale, eventually uncovering more than 50,000 flakes, at least four artifact concentration areas, several hundred stone tools and mammoth ivory. LaPrele was no longer just a kill site but a camp where humans had lived.

29:15 Hearths and tent walls left fingerprints in the sediment
LaPrele's most striking find is four "hearth-centered areas." In Block B, the team found no obvious ash or oxidized traces, but burned bone and flakes concentrated in a small patch, indicating a hearth once stood there. Even better is the spatial analysis: if you look down at a tent from above, the hearth is at the center, activity-dense areas surround it, then an open space for walking, and near the tent wall objects pile up — because the wall is a barrier to artifact movement. Block B's artifact distribution shows exactly this "bullseye" pattern, indicating an interior space. In the same area they also found a roughly 1.5-by-2-meter scatter of ochre (hematite) pigment matching the wall's position, suggesting people painted by the fire.

39:25 The bone needles were made from red fox and felid bone
The team used ZooMS (Zooarchaeology by Mass Spectrometry) to analyze bone needles and possible bone beads; the method extracts proteins from extremely small bone samples to identify the animal species. The results were unexpected: many needles were made from hare bone, but one was red fox and another tested as felid — not a domestic cat, but some wild felid. Mackey notes these are all fur-bearing animals, and their bone thickness may have been just right for needles. More importantly, these animals were probably caught in traps rather than hunted with spears. That means Clovis people weren't hunting mammoths 24 hours a day; they were also taking more common small prey.

44:32 Were Clovis people mammoth specialists or omnivores
About 15 widely accepted Clovis sites in North America are associated with megafauna, mostly proboscideans (mammoth, mastodon, gomphothere), plus horse and camel. But Mackey points out that only about 30 to 40 sites truly define our understanding of Clovis, while thousands of Clovis spear points have been found on the surface, lacking context. That raises a core debate: were they mammoth-hunting specialists, or omnivores with a broader diet? Small animals, fish and plant remains preserve less well and are less often systematically sought. Mackey is studying plant remains, and she notes archaeologists usually look for plants only in hearths, and how many places in the Clovis record have actually been looked at is itself a problem.

50:00 Mammoth extinction: did humans push, or was climate the main driver
The classic "overkill" debate: 35 genera of megafauna went extinct at the end of the Ice Age, and how much was human versus environmental? Mackey says she takes a middle path, believing both contributed. She considers mammoths the strongest candidate for the overkill hypothesis, because mammoth sites are numerous, the animals were large and had low reproductive rates, making them more vulnerable to hunting. But she also notes overkill doesn't necessarily mean humans hunted all 35 genera; hunting may have upset the balance through trophic cascades. Interestingly, paleoecologists lean toward "humans did it," while archaeologists lean more toward "the environment did it."

53:12 Clovis human bone barely exists
Apart from a single case of ancestral remains attributed to Clovis at the Anzick site in Montana, we have almost no Clovis human bone. Mackey doesn't find this surprising: population density was extremely low, 13,000-year-old sites are inherently extremely hard to preserve, and these groups were highly mobile, so we don't know their burial practices. She also stresses that Clovis people are the ancestors of millions of Indigenous people in the Americas today, and any related research must proceed on the basis of consultation and collaboration.

item.title: 40,000 Ottomans Lay Siege to Malta — and Lose to a Few Hundred Knights
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-historyhit-奥斯曼四万大军围攻马耳他-为何败给几百骑士/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-historyhit-奥斯曼四万大军围攻马耳他-为何败给几百骑士/
item.description: In 1565 an Ottoman fleet of 180 ships and 40,000 men besieged Malta, defended by roughly 500 knights and a few thousand Maltese. Fort St Elmo held out for a month before falling, but the siege dragged on until Sicilian reinforcements landed in September and the Ottomans withdrew.
item.content:encoded:
In 1565 an Ottoman fleet of 180 ships and 40,000 men besieged Malta, defended by roughly 500 knights and a few thousand Maltese. Fort St Elmo held out for a month before falling, but the siege dragged on until Sicilian reinforcements landed in September and the Ottomans withdrew.

This episode is on-location siege narrative — vivid but light on analysis. If you want the mechanics of why Malta held, the middle and later sections on scorched earth and disinformation are the most valuable.

3:02 Malta's value is its position, not its resources
Malta sits almost exactly in the middle of the Mediterranean: 80 km north of Sicily, hard against North Africa to the south, and roughly equidistant from Gibraltar and the Suez Canal. Whoever controls Malta controls the trade routes. The Grand Harbour, where Valletta now stands, is a rare natural deep-water port that is safe to anchor in whatever direction the wind blows. The Knights did not initially want Malta — there was no existing fortress and no resources — and only took it because the first Grand Master insisted on having a foothold.

7:10 What the Knights brought was the Italian bastion
The Knights brought Italian-style military architecture (Traccia Italiana) to Malta: no longer the tall medieval castle, but low, sloped, outward-projecting bastions with thick walls packed with earth to absorb the impact of gunpowder artillery. Fort St Angelo got the first bastion. By 1552 the Knights had realised how dangerous their position was, and the Grand Master Domades pushed hard for fortifications. A chain was also strung underwater between St Angelo and Fort St Michael at Senglea, serving much like a WWII anti-submarine net to block ships.

11:26 What the defenders waited for was a fleet on the horizon
On 18 May 1565 the garrison of Fort St Elmo saw a vast fleet approaching on the horizon, signalled at once, and the whole island went to war footing. The defenders numbered about 10,000 in total, including knights, Maltese civilians and mercenaries hired from Italy. This was not a war you could surrender in: the losers would be killed or sold as slaves, so for many it was a fight to the death. The Ottomans, for their part, arrived thinking they would take the place in a few days and move on to the next target, and set their first objective on Fort St Elmo.

13:33 Fort St Elmo held only a month, but it tied the Ottomans down
The Ottoman fleet — about 190 ships and an estimated 35,000 soldiers — arrived at the Grand Harbour and did not strike directly at the Knights' headquarters at St Angelo, but first attacked Fort St Elmo, which guarded the entrances to both harbours. Fire opened on 27 May, with hundreds of guns bombarding almost without pause and reducing the walls to rubble; every night the Knights patched the breaches, hauled ammunition and treated the wounded, then fought again the next day. Fort St Elmo had been thrown up in only about six months, its works were not good enough, and the Ottomans found it comparatively easy to scale and dismantle. The Grand Master's strategy was simply to keep the Ottomans attacking and keep bleeding them. By the night of 22 June the fort was a ruin, and the surviving garrison said Mass in the chapel, preparing not for victory but for death. At noon on 23 June the last knights died fighting, and Fort St Elmo fell.

16:46 Both sides used corpses to send a message
This was a war with no room for surrender. After the last defenders of Fort St Elmo were killed, the Ottomans cut off their heads and lashed the bodies to rafts in the shape of a cross, then set them adrift as a warning to the Grand Master of what was coming. The Grand Master is said to have fired Ottoman heads back from the guns of St Angelo in reply. On 15 July the Ottomans tried to attack Senglea, but below St Angelo at sea level there was a small battery the Ottomans had not spotted; when it opened fire they were caught completely off guard, and nearly all the attacking boats were sunk.

18:51 Scorched earth broke the Ottomans first
By July the Knights' side was still reasonably supplied; it was the Ottomans who had the problem. The Knights and the Maltese waged scorched earth, burning everything as they withdrew, so the Ottomans could find no food at all. It was the height of summer, the heat was punishing, and Ottoman morale began to collapse into panic. The Grand Master's tactic was to wear down the enemy's manpower and will until they gave up on their own. One Ottoman leader is said to have remarked that if St Elmo had taken this long, what would St Angelo cost? Maltese civilians took part in large numbers too, including women who served in nursing and in combat.

22:03 A tiny cavalry force scared off an Ottomans army on the brink of winning
In early August the Ottomans attacked Birgu and Senglea at the same time, at one point breaking through the walls and fighting a bloody melee in the streets, and they looked to have the upper hand. The Knights countered with a ruse: a commander at Mdina, the inland Maltese fortress city, sent out a very small force of Maltese cavalry, which raided the Ottoman field hospital and supply camp. Rumour spread fast through the Ottoman army that a huge relief force had arrived. The Ottoman commander Mustafa Pasha broke off the assault and withdrew on the edge of victory. By late August both sides were locked in a war of attrition, with disease, hunger and casualties mounting, and the Ottomans had lost experienced commanders such as Dragut.

23:03 The relief came, but the Ottoman Empire was not broken
On 7 September 1565, 8,000 Spanish, Italian and Sicilian troops sent by Don Garcia in the name of Philip II of Spain landed on Malta from Sicily and advanced on the exhausted Ottoman army. The Knights had been begging for help for weeks, and the relief was late but it came. The Ottomans formally surrendered. But Kirsty stresses that this did not weaken the Ottoman Empire's power or legitimacy — it continued as an empire for a long time afterwards, and people today tend to inflate the significance of this victory. After the siege the Knights immediately set about building the new city of Valletta and repairing Fort St Elmo; the Grand Master La Valette died before he saw the city finished.

item.title: The British Expedition to Ethiopia: A Hostage Crisis Won With Railways and Elephants
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-restishistory-英国远征埃塞俄比亚-一场用铁路和大象打赢的人质危机/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-restishistory-英国远征埃塞俄比亚-一场用铁路和大象打赢的人质危机/
item.description: In 1868 Britain spent £10 million, shipped in 44 elephants and 20 miles of railway track to rescue a few dozen hostages, using breech-loading rifles against spears to produce a massacre — then withdrew immediately, leaving Ethiopia to two decades of civil war.
item.content:encoded:
In 1868 Britain spent £10 million, shipped in 44 elephants and 20 miles of railway track to rescue a few dozen hostages, using breech-loading rifles against spears to produce a massacre — then withdrew immediately, leaving Ethiopia to two decades of civil war.

The storytelling is excellent, but the information density is not high; suited to anyone who wants a complete case study of how an imperial intervention ends, rather than an analytical framework.

5:12 Face was worth more than the hostages
The Derby cabinet decided to send troops not for humanitarian reasons, but because Britain could not be humiliated by an African king in front of its subjects in India and Aden. The episode states plainly that if you asked Derby or Disraeli, they cared far more about British prestige than about those few missionaries. Rescuing the hostages was a by-product; prestige was the main product. That judgment determined everything that followed: Napier's orders were to go in, get the hostages, and come out — never occupy, never install a puppet.

11:18 Napier worked the supply line backwards from the endpoint
Napier was an engineer by training, and his planning ran in reverse: to rescue the hostages he needed 5,000 men, those 5,000 men needed hundreds of miles of supply line, so he added another 7,000 to guard the line, and then he needed a coastal base and two sea routes. He was mobilising the resources of an entire empire — Liverpool, Woolwich, Chatham, Bombay, Madras. The episode quotes Philip Marsden's book saying that everyone from quartermasters to cooks to porters went to work to free the hostages held by the ‘gorilla king’. This was an expedition run as an engineering project.

14:21 The expedition's hard currency was Austrian silver
In East Africa the only universally accepted currency was the Austrian Maria Theresa thaler, first minted in 1741, with the 1780 version the most sought after. Napier first sent men to Central Europe to buy up old coins, then sent men to the official mint in Vienna to exchange British silver for 20,000 coins struck each week specifically for the expedition. The episode says this coin was still circulating locally into the 1950s. A British expeditionary force had to rely on Habsburg silver two centuries old to buy food and bribe local warlords.

18:37 44 elephants and 20 miles of track came ashore
By the new year of 1868 the British had landed 13,000 soldiers, 20 miles of railway track and 44 elephants — the elephants carried across the Indian Ocean in specially reinforced transport ships, seven more than Hannibal had. Engineers blasted paths up cliffs, first climbing to 8,000 feet, then crossing gorges and ravines for 350 miles to Magdala. They also laid copper telegraph wire the whole way, running field telegraph up to the advance guard. The episode says this may have been the most technologically advanced military operation in history.

21:44 Napier bought the road with gifts
The road to Magdala ran through the territory of Ras Kassa, king of Tigray. Napier halted to wait for him, drew up his troops in salute, invited him to inspect the artillery, presented Arabian horses, rifles and glassware, and promised that his troops would not loot or steal, that he would pay for every sack of grain, and that he offered Queen Victoria's friendship. Kassa gave him a lion-skin cloak in return and promised weekly grain deliveries. The episode points out an understanding that was never written down: Kassa expected Napier to finish Teodros for good, and that was the bargain.

37:20 Drunk, Teodros threw three hundred people off a cliff
On the Thursday before Easter, Teodros drank too much and went to sleep after lunch. At four in the afternoon he was woken by the sound of prisoners complaining that their shackles were being removed too slowly. Enraged, he called for a sword, stabbed two prisoners to death on the spot, then ordered the remaining three hundred or so thrown off the cliff one by one, with guards sent down afterwards to finish them off. The whole process lasted two hours. That night a servant heard him praying to God, admitting he had been drunk when he gave the order for the massacre and asking not to be blamed for it.

46:49 Breech-loaders turned a spear charge into a massacre
The Abyssinians had charged rifle lines before, and they knew riflemen took a long time to reload after firing, so you could rush them in that gap. But this time the British were equipped for the first time with the Snider breech-loading rifle, which could be reloaded in seconds, and the whole line could fire 30 to 40 rounds a second with no break in the fire. The chiefs and captains at the front were the first to fall because they wore bright red shirts. The result: roughly a thousand Abyssinians dead and thousands wounded, against two British dead and about twenty wounded.

56:00 Refusing the cattle meant refusing peace
Teodros sent a thousand cattle and five hundred sheep as a gesture of peace, but Napier refused them. The episode explains why: by local custom, accepting those animals meant accepting peace and letting the matter end there. Seeing Napier drive the cattle and sheep back, Teodros bitterly told his courtiers that these people had got what they wanted and now wanted his life. That turn locked in the suicidal ending.

item.title: Australia Regulates Supplements Like Drugs, but Nobody Checks Whether They Work
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-bizthisway-澳洲保健品监管像药-但没人管它有没有效/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-bizthisway-澳洲保健品监管像药-但没人管它有没有效/
item.description: Australia puts supplements and pharmaceuticals under the same agency, which looks strict; but efficacy is neither reviewed before market nor tested on the production line — the impression of "good" was implanted by marketing and cross-border policy.
item.content:encoded:
Australia puts supplements and pharmaceuticals under the same agency, which looks strict; but efficacy is neither reviewed before market nor tested on the production line — the impression of "good" was implanted by marketing and cross-border policy.

The first half's regulatory breakdown is solid, and the back half's chain from marketing to daigou policy is complete; but the middle section has a lot of transcription garbage, so the information density is uneven.

4:00 Australians taking pills is a tradition
The soil for Australia's supplement industry isn't the natural environment, it's four social habits: a sparse population that self-medicates, pharmacists who also diagnose and dispense, naturopathic industry organisations dating to the 1920s, and health food stores resembling food-as-medicine shops. Stack those four together and Australians take it for granted that you solve health problems without going to the hospital. Black Moth (澳佳宝) started as a naturopathic clinic; only after the second generation took over did it translate that into products the mainstream system could recognise — turning "take a spoonful of fish oil a day" into a standardised fish oil capsule, for instance.

12:05 The contract manufacturers are the industry's foundation
Pen Pharmaceuticals, which appeared in 1974, was Australia's first company focused on contract manufacturing for supplements, and by around 2003 it was producing roughly 70% of Australia's vitamins, minerals and herbal products. Its value lay in process know-how: tablets, compound ingredients, the rubber-and-oil seal on soft capsules, the mixing uniformity of powders, the stability of liquids — each is its own set of solutions. In the 1980s and 90s a new generation of contract manufacturers extended service in both directions, moving from pure production (CMO) to CDMO covering formulation, ingredients, trial production, labelling, packaging, testing, and registration for export. The brand only has to hand over a concept, and the factory can turn it into a product ready to sell.

15:05 Registration means nobody looks before it hits the market
Australia legislated in 1989, putting the TGA in charge of both pharmaceuticals and supplements, and all products must obtain an AUST number. Most supplements fall into the AUSTL category: only low-risk ingredients permitted by the TGA, only low-level health claims, and a company gets the number just by applying — the TGA does no pre-market review, only post-market spot checks. By around 2010 Australia had roughly ten thousand complementary medicines, of which nearly 98% sat in this registration system. Only prescription drugs, over-the-counter drugs and a small number of high-risk supplements enter the AUSTR tier, which requires the TGA to assess safety, quality and efficacy in advance.

20:06 It looks strict, but in practice it is loose
Put the contract manufacturing and regulatory lines together and you see that GMP only guarantees the factory produces consistently to the standard the brand gives it, and that problems can be traced to a batch for recall — it is not itself responsible for whether the product works. The TGA side only handles declarations and issuing licence numbers; efficacy is explained by the brand itself. So the claim that "Australia regulates supplements like drugs" is not wrong in itself, but it is misleading: the method of control is the same, while the degree of control over the efficacy part differs enormously. The whole system exercises no effective upfront oversight of a product's actual effect, and there is a risk of disconnect between the brand and the product's efficacy.

25:08 The marketing was copied from Centrum, not invented
CEO Radek Sali, who took over in 2008, did not conjure a marketing plan out of thin air. He did industry research and found the best seller among peers was Centrum, and the feedback from retailers was: Centrum didn't give the channel much margin, but it was on TV blasting ads all year, had great athlete endorsements, and consumers walked into the pharmacy asking for it by name. Sali wanted to replicate that at Swisse. He started with Australia's national sport, cricket — the men's team captain, buying very short ad slots only during the hottest summer cricket broadcasts, so a limited budget could still appear at key moments. But the female-dominated sales channel wasn't moved; one buyer didn't watch cricket herself and didn't know the player. He asked his mother what shows she liked, and she said a dance variety show, and the strategy pivoted to spoken endorsements in entertainment content.

26:09 Selling health as a lifestyle
Swisse's bigger promotional push drew on Oprah and Ellen, and signed actress Nicole Kidman for three years, extending its reach from Australia to the United States. By 2012 Swisse had 25 brand ambassadors, had shot more than 80 TV commercials in the previous 12 months, and reached annual revenue of 183 million Australian dollars, with marketing spend of 40 to 50 million Australian dollars a year — said at one point to be the highest marketing spend of any consumer brand in all of Australia. Its ads didn't stress efficacy or ingredients; they mainly presented a state of being energetic, positively disciplined and good-looking — turning health into a lifestyle consumers aspire to. In 2012 Swisse took more than 20% market share in Australian supermarket channels and more than 10% in pharmacy channels.

32:14 The growth was found in Chinese pharmacies
Swisse's expensive push into the US market was not a success, and back home in Australia it found that Swisse sold extremely well in pharmacies in Chinese-populated areas — some stores selling at ten times the level of an ordinary store — because students and Chinese immigrants bought it in bulk to carry back to China or resell online, that is, daigou. Two policy shifts came in 2015: in March the Hangzhou cross-border e-commerce comprehensive pilot zone was approved, and in June China and Australia signed a free trade agreement, which took effect that December. The FTA mainly affected ordinary trade; Australian official statistics put the tariff on vitamins and supplements generally at 3% to 10%, while Black Moth itself estimated an average rate of 20%, and after the agreement it was said at the time that this could fall to zero within four years. Cross-border e-commerce goes through bonded warehouses, platforms buy in bulk, logistics time and cost drop sharply, and such goods are treated in policy as for personal use, so they don't have to go through the registration and filing process for supplement imports.

35:16 The brand was bought; the impression stayed put
In September 2015 Hong Kong-listed Biostime completed the acquisition of a controlling stake in Swisse, and two years later completed a full buyout, a deal of about 1.7 billion Australian dollars, or 8.7 billion yuan. For Swisse the deal carried little premium; for Biostime it added a large chunk of business revenue and imagination. Now all those Swisse ads in Hunan TV variety shows are, in theory, a Chinese supplement company spending money, yet the brand can still say it is an Australian supplement brand, and consumers can still apply their old vague good impression of Australia to it — a large proportion of the acquisition's core value settles in brand goodwill.

item.title: Lenin Designed the Terror Machine; Stalin Just Took It Over
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-empirehist-列宁设计了恐怖机器-斯大林只是接手了它/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-empirehist-列宁设计了恐怖机器-斯大林只是接手了它/
item.description: The secret police, the labour camps and the one-party system were all architecture Lenin left behind. What Stalin did was turn it into a personal instrument of power — the first thing he did as General Secretary was stuff his own people into key posts.
item.content:encoded:
The secret police, the labour camps and the one-party system were all architecture Lenin left behind. What Stalin did was turn it into a personal instrument of power — the first thing he did as General Secretary was stuff his own people into key posts.

This episode gets the attribution of the Soviet terror system straight: it wasn't invented out of thin air by Stalin, it was a stage Lenin built and Stalin performed on. The back half, on Lenin's testament and the funeral details, is dense with information.

2:06 In 1917 Stalin was a man nobody noticed
The episode opens by recalling the impression left by the previous instalment: Stalin was a terrible speaker and a slow theorist, and no one would have guessed he was the next dictator. Guest Giles Milton confirms that judgement and adds a key detail — Stalin rarely appeared in public and was not well known in Russia; he hated public speaking because his Georgian accent was so heavy. This explains how he was later able to accumulate power quietly: nobody treated him as a threat.

4:11 Churchill once wanted to wipe out the Red Army with gas
During the civil war, Britain, France, the US and Japan all backed the Whites. Churchill, as Minister of Munitions in 1919, pushed Britain to send troops and weapons to Russia against the Reds. More striking still, Britain had developed a lethal chemical weapon late in the First World War, and Churchill thought it more humane than the bloody slaughter in the trenches, so he sent it to use against Trotsky's Red Army. Because of the atmospheric conditions in northern Russia the gas worked poorly, and the whole stock was eventually dumped into the White Sea. This history explains how hard it was when Churchill allied with Stalin in 1941 — he himself was one of the men who had wanted to get rid of Stalin back then.

9:27 The terror machine's architecture was Lenin's legacy
Many people put the Cheka, the labour camps and the one-party system down to Stalin, saying he built them while serving as a political commissar in the civil war. Giles argues this completely misunderstands Lenin's role: it was Lenin who built this architecture, and Stalin merely took it later and used it for his own political career. The Cheka was the secret police, which later became the more familiar KGB — surveillance, arrest, torture, execution. The host sums it up: when we look back at history we often say Stalin was a corrosive influence, that he brought the terror, but the architecture was in fact Lenin's bequest.

10:27 Tsaritsyn: Stalin arrested a front-line general
Trotsky appointed Snezarev, a general from the former tsarist army, to command the Tsaritsyn campaign — a typical Trotsky move of using old officers, and one that put him directly in conflict with Stalin. Stalin, as political commissar, arrested the general and all his subordinate officers and locked them on a barge on the Volga. It is said his intention was to sink the boat and drown them. Trotsky was furious when he found out and ordered the general released immediately. This was the first round in the struggle between Trotsky and Stalin, and Trotsky won big. But Stalin later told the story as one of the great civil-war battles in which he personally went to the front, and Tsaritsyn was later renamed Stalingrad.

16:44 Whenever Stalin was unhappy he threatened to resign
Giles gives a detail that does not fit Stalin's later image: whenever things went badly, for instance when he failed to get authorisation at Tsaritsyn to liquidate Trotsky, he threatened to resign. He wrote a letter saying that without this, my work on the Southern Front would become meaningless and unnecessary, and that this gave him the right or the obligation to go even to the devil rather than stay on the Southern Front. The Politburo read the letter, grew tired of it, and said, no, Joseph, stay, we all love you. He was a sulker. The picture fixes something in the reader's mind: the early Stalin used emotional blackmail, not terror.

29:12 Nobody thought much of the job of General Secretary
In April 1922 Stalin was appointed General Secretary. Today the title means supreme power in the state, but at the time it was just a functional description, tedious work. Stalin understood: handled properly, the post gave him complete control of the party. He could plant his own people in key positions and clear out everyone who supported Trotsky. From the day he took it over he made full use of the position, and already had one eye on the future — Lenin's health was poor, he was thinking about who would succeed Lenin, and now he had the chance to fill the party with supporters so that when Lenin died he would be in an advantageous position.

32:13 Stalin's apology letter: says sorry without admitting fault
Stalin telephoned Lenin's home. Lenin was gravely ill, and Stalin accused Nadezhda of discussing politics with Lenin as he was dying, saying it was unforgivable. Nadezhda told Lenin, Lenin was enraged, and insisted Stalin write a letter of apology. The letter is a marvel: Stalin apologises without apologising — if you think I offended her, then I apologise, but I do not think I really offended her, so there is nothing to apologise for. Lenin was even angrier. On 4 January 1923 Lenin wrote down his assessment of Stalin: Stalin is too rude, and this defect, entirely tolerable in our internal and comradely relations, becomes intolerable in the post of General Secretary, and he therefore proposed that the comrades find a way to remove Stalin and replace him with someone else.

35:21 If Lenin hadn't died, Stalin would have put him in prison
Lenin's political life ended with his stroke, and he died ten days later. His wife, Nadezhda Krupskaya, said the most famous thing of all: if Lenin had not died in 1924, he would have been serving time in one of Stalin's prisons. She saw that Stalin was moving against Lenin as he rose. Giles thinks it very likely, because Stalin was absolutely ruthless towards anyone he believed was not on his side. Lenin wanted a simple burial; Stalin decided not to bury him but to embalm and preserve him and put him on permanent display. Within hours of Lenin's death they began draining his fluids and removing his organs, and the heart was never found again.

item.title: Solo Founders Aren't Alone: The Relationship Is the Product
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-solofounders-单人创始人不是一个人-关系才是产品/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-solofounders-单人创始人不是一个人-关系才是产品/
item.description: 85% of startups die because the relationship didn't work, not because the product idea was bad. Being a solo founder really means being a solo artist — treating relationships as the main job, not actually carrying it all alone.
item.content:encoded:
85% of startups die because the relationship didn't work, not because the product idea was bad. Being a solo founder really means being a solo artist — treating relationships as the main job, not actually carrying it all alone.

This episode has medium information density, but Dave Morin uses three cases — OpenClaw, Pulsia and Ramble — to explain clearly what solo founders actually survive on. The mechanics in the second half are worth more than the motivational talk in the first.

4:04 The share of solo-founded startups doubled in five years
Carta data shows that roughly 40% of companies this year were founded by a single person, up from under 25% five years ago. Dave Morin doesn't think this is an accident: social media means you hardly feel alone for any waking hour, and AI has become a huge input source over the past two or three years. You used to lie in bed texting friends; now you talk to AI, explore your own ideas and get input on what to do tomorrow. The "internal craft" of starting a company has also gone from a dark art held by a few to something YouTube and ChatGPT can teach.

10:06 Most startups die from relationships, not products
Dave puts it bluntly: most startups fail because the relationship didn't work, not because the product idea was bad or the market didn't exist. He compares it to a band breaking up — you never get to hear the music you loved again. When your favourite app suddenly gets a redesign and the UI becomes infuriating, behind it is often that the "band" changed, the relationships changed, the people who made it changed. So he says the relationship is, in a sense, the product itself.

16:11 Designing the team matters as much as designing the product
When Steve Jobs died, Dave was working on Path, Jony Ive was helping him, and he was helping Jony with some Apple work. Jony said something to him that he still remembers: designing the team matters as much as designing the product.
