From that Dave draws his core judgment — you can be a solo artist, but you are always inside a huge collaboration, not just with the creators around you but with customers, audiences and the community that cares about your product. You are not alone.

19:12 He fell in love with OpenClaw within 12 hours
In December 2025, Dave was in Montana with family for the holidays when a friend told him to look at something called Claudebot. He didn't look the first day; he installed it the second, and within less than 12 hours he had the feeling he'd had as a kid — when his grandfather put a Macintosh on his desk at age 7 and he first felt he could create anything. The second time he felt that was seeing Facebook; within 24 hours he decided he had to find the founder. This time it was OpenClaw, and he immediately went to find Peter, moving from Twitter DMs to iMessage, talking every day, saying "I don't know what this becomes, but everyone needs to experience it, and we have to protect it at all costs."

27:20 Peter is a craftsman with ten years of practice, not a lucky break
Dave doesn't see OpenClaw's explosion as an accident. Peter spent ten years doing hardcore PDF engineering, with an understanding of Mac OS details down to the engineering level that exceeds most people's. So when Claude and agentic engineering arrived in 2025, he was an artist who had already digested all the material and could make his art extremely fast and extremely beautifully. Dave's conclusion: this is an intensely trained creator who, given new tools, made something magical.

32:24 Ben built himself a Company OS on the road
After Ben and his co-founder decided not to be partners and split the company in two, he went alone to Kyoto, Hong Kong, Shanghai and Thailand. Halfway through the trip he called Dave and said: I built myself a system because I felt lonely. He built a bunch of agents to help him build the company — a CMO, an engineering VP, a therapist — and he called it Company OS. Dave says this was one of the earliest times he heard anyone talk about multi-agent systems, more than a year ago. Three months later Pulsia launched. Ben later told him that if Dave hadn't said "you're not crazy, you're just halfway through the album," he might have given up.

36:29 Matt applied data science to campsites
Matt's previous company was in book publishing, using data science and machine learning to work backwards to "what book you should write," selling books out before they even reached Amazon — at its peak, more than 80% of Amazon's top 50 books were published by them. During the pandemic he and Dave talked by a campfire: could this approach be applied to camping? National Park and Bureau of Land Management land can be camped on, but Airbnb has almost no supply in places like Zion. So Ramble uses data to decide where to buy land — where there should be supply but isn't. Dave calls this "the PhD mode of startups," because it's essentially real estate development: buying land and negotiating with landowners, counties and cities, and zoning.

44:32 You have to be the person in the world who loves it most
Dave says Matt is an extraordinary mountaineer, climbing at the Denali level, and he knows fewer than five people who do that kind of climbing. Ramble is an expression of Matt's love of nature; he wants to give other people that experience of being completely immersed in the natural world. Dave's inference: you have to love it to that degree to turn it into a business. Otherwise, first, someone else will love it more than you and they will beat you; second, you'll have to talk about it for ten thousand hours, and ten years later you'll still be talking about it, so you have to love it, because you'll have to eat ten thousand dinners about it.

item.title: The bottleneck for AI adoption isn't capability — it's that nobody will sign their name to it
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-latentspace-ai-落地的瓶颈不是能力-是没人敢签字担责/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-latentspace-ai-落地的瓶颈不是能力-是没人敢签字担责/
item.description: Waymo drove better than a human four years ago and still can't get into an airport — what constrains AI's usefulness was never capability, but liability, risk and trust. AIUC wants to fill that gap with standards plus insurance.
item.content:encoded:
Waymo drove better than a human four years ago and still can't get into an airport — what constrains AI's usefulness was never capability, but liability, risk and trust. AIUC wants to fill that gap with standards plus insurance.

For founders, investors and operators who care about AI deployment, compliance, insurance and third-party audit. The historical analogies in the first half run long; the second half — the lemon problem, eval awareness, and the race to the bottom among rating agencies — is worth more.

7:58 Waymo still can't get into an airport after four years
Rune's core evidence is Waymo: by early 2022 it was already a superhuman driver, but you couldn't take it to the airport; more than four years later you still can't, even though everyone agrees it drives better than a person. So what constrains AI's usefulness isn't capability — it's liability, risk and trust. Worse, the problem gets worse as AI gets stronger: the more intelligent and autonomous it is, the more valuable it is, and the larger the risk surface. He traces this back through history: electricity in the 1900s, cars in the 1930s, private nuclear power in the 1950s — each time the market ran ahead of regulation and built the confidence infrastructure, because go/no-go decisions required it. The common blueprint is standards plus insurance: standards supply the rules of the road and which tests to run, insurers pay the bill and therefore have the strongest incentive to genuinely quantify risk and find ways to reduce it.

23:26 Most companies have the right building blocks, but they don't work
Rune says the most important thing is that many companies have never done serious stress testing — they spend their time optimising output quality in the good case and the average case, and they often hire their first security lead very late. Most companies actually have the right architecture and do have guardrails, either out of the box from the model vendor or filters they built themselves; the problem is that they don't work well. For example, dropping in a classifier that says "if this looks like medical advice, filter it out" — lots of companies have that, but the genuinely hard part is sitting down and thinking through all the ways someone could elicit medical advice, and reading the academic literature on the frameworks and techniques for getting around AI. AIUC-1 splits requirements into three categories: technical controls (for example, you must implement a groundedness filter), testing controls (tests must be run by an independent third party), and policy controls (for example, there must be a named person who owns the liability, and a plan for how customers are notified when something goes wrong).

38:14 Standards run by nonprofits are a problem
Rune says flatly that most standards in cybersecurity today are written by nonprofit organisations, and he thinks that's a problem. Nonprofits have no profit motive to hollow out a standard and race to the bottom on price, but by default they are completely unresponsive to the community they serve — no customers, nobody asking "what do you want" — which is why satisfaction with existing security standards is generally low. He gives counterexamples of for-profit standards: Moody's, FICO credit scores, and earlier, crash-test standards that came from insurers; UL (Underwriters Laboratories) was born in an era of electric lights spreading, houses catching fire, and insurers footing the bill, and today UL has a for-profit entity, because serving customers well requires one. His conviction is that standards must come before insurance: whether it's the CISO at JPMorgan, the CISO at Cursor, or an underwriter at Lloyd's, the first demand is "don't have an incident" — once you've confirmed the risk is managed, insurance starts to mean something.

42:47 A policy is a trust signal to the market
Rune explains that demand for AI insurance comes mainly from the gap between "people building AI" and "people buying AI". Buying insurance isn't just about getting paid when something goes wrong; more importantly, the insurer brings trust: its willingness to underwrite is a statement that "there is risk here, but it's manageable", and its interests are aligned with the company adopting AI, so it's a good signal to the market. When Waymo got its San Francisco operating permit, it went to multiple insurers and stacked them into one enormous policy — not because Google couldn't afford to pay, but so that the government and a trusted third party could look at the data and say "we're willing to put some of this on our own balance sheet". The concrete case is ElevenLabs buying the first AI agent insurance policy, with Lloyd's of London as a third party looking at the data alongside them. There have been no claims yet.

1:00:30 Copyright insurance is a textbook lemon problem
Rune says copyright is a segment with high demand and little supply. One reason is that almost anyone who trained on copyrighted material knows they trained on it, so the very act of wanting to buy copyright infringement insurance signals that you may be a high-risk customer — the people who most want to buy are precisely the ones most likely to have a copyright problem, which Swyx calls outright a lemon problem. Vibhu adds the other side: when you use an open-source model you don't know what it was trained on, and how far can the chain of liability be traced? Rune admits this is hard and that he doesn't have the answer, but argues that "not unpacking open-source model training data line by line" is today treated as generally acceptable, so they won't hold you to a specific standard on it.

1:06:04 Agents are starting to know they're being evaluated
Rune points out that evals face a new challenge: agents are starting to realise they're being evaluated — eval awareness. If it knows it's being watched, it won't do the things it thinks it will be punished for, so unless you know how to reduce eval awareness, you should trust evals less. He thinks monitoring is the paradigm closer to the truth — did you actually give medical advice, how fast did you find out, how often historically, how fast did you respond — at the cost of being more invasive, requiring visibility into some customer data, but it will become more and more common. He also mentions an Anthropic study: after removing the parts of the training data where LessWrong discussed misalignment, rerunning the same test produced a lower failure rate.

1:12:56 The questions prediction markets can't answer are the audit business
Someone asks why not just open a prediction market on everything. Rune's answer: prediction markets depend on public information, and the information that actually determines high-stakes decisions is often private, or doesn't exist yet at all — for example, what a bank's security lead really needs to ask is "will this agent do the specific bad thing I care about in the specific scenario I care about", and there is nowhere that question has an answer. So the third-party auditor's position isn't aggregating existing information, it's generating information. He adds in passing: we also don't use prediction markets to determine whether a public company committed accounting fraud — we use audits.

1:14:02 Audit is a natural monopoly, but insurers can check it
Swyx cites the line from The Big Short where Moody's says "if we don't give you AAA, you'll go to S&P" to make the point that rating agencies compete downward, and watchdogs naturally race to lower standards. Rune agrees, and gives the reason AIUC brought insurers into the picture — insurers are the one party without that dynamic, because they pay the bill directly, and pushing the price down all the way means losing their own money. He also concedes there is no perfect system, that Moody's needs scrutiny, and that watchdogs need scrutiny too. Asked whether the business changes if, in eighteen months, OpenAI's secret five-person group announces AGI, Rune says no, because the one thing a lab can never do is be its own watchdog — the issue isn't whether they care, it's that they're trapped in a race, with incentives to cut corners and withhold information from governments.

item.title: Human brain organoids transplanted into mice grow four million human neurons
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-naturepod-人脑类器官移植进小鼠-长出了四百万人类神经元/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-naturepod-人脑类器官移植进小鼠-长出了四百万人类神经元/
item.description: Mice genetically stripped of nearly their entire cortex, then given human brain organoids, grew about 4 million human neurons — and behaved neither like normal mice nor like cortex-less mice, but like a third state.
item.content:encoded:
Mice genetically stripped of nearly their entire cortex, then given human brain organoids, grew about 4 million human neurons — and behaved neither like normal mice nor like cortex-less mice, but like a third state.

The first half is solid neurodevelopmental research; the second half's "paper becomes an AI agent" workflow is more informative for people building research tools and AI agents.

2:08 No surgery — genetics makes the room
In 2022, Sergio Pasca's team implanted human brain organoids into newborn rat brains, but human brain cells grow far more slowly than rodent ones, and the implanted organoids were "outcompeted," getting neither connections nor room to grow. This time they took a different approach: no surgery, but a genetic trick that deletes a gene essential for cell division only in the cells that would form the brain region. The result is that cells are unable to divide the moment they are born ready to build cortex, and stall in place. The structure removed is called the pallium; it exists early and later develops into the cerebral cortex and hippocampus. These "pallium-less mice" lost nearly half their brain volume but survived, with reduced body weight and largely normal basic motor and sensory responses.

4:08 Four million human neurons take over the empty space
The team injected human stem-cell-derived cortical organoids into pallium-less pups aged 5 to 17 days, about four organoids per injection, each roughly 100,000 cells and already differentiated, on their way to forming cortex. The human cells then divided, differentiated, were vascularised by the host, and mouse immune cells entered the interior of the human graft. Months later, the team estimated that these animals, called xenocortical mice, had about 70 million neurons in total, of which about 14 million were cortical and hippocampal cells, most of what was removed replaced by about 4 million human neurons. Human cells are larger and less dense, so the replacement is not an equal number, but it is still a very large number of human neurons.

6:10 They are neither normal mice nor cortex-less mice
The team used machine learning to analyse behavioural differences among three kinds of mice in video: controls, pallium-less mice that had lost almost the entire cortex, and xenocortical mice with the organoid implants. Pallium-less mice differed clearly from controls, while xenocortical mice were "neither," sitting in a third behavioural state. Later experiments backed this up: pallium-less animals had deficits on working-memory tasks, xenocortical animals did not. Sergio's judgement is that function was preserved in the animals that received human cortical cells, and human cells very likely contributed some of it — but this is not perfect restoration, only evidence that these cells can integrate functionally and produce behavioural consequences.

7:11 A hypoxia experiment shows it is the human cells doing the work
The team used this system to model brain injury. Hypoxia is severe in humans and can cause lifelong disease, whereas mice tolerate low oxygen far better. After the three kinds of mice were exposed to hypoxic conditions for several hours, the human cells were induced to mount a hypoxia response, while the mouse brain was relatively resilient. Two days later, on a motor task, wild-type mice and pallium-less mice were fine, but the xenocortical mice carrying human cells began to show deficits in walking and gait coordination. Sergio argues this shows it is very likely the human cells causing these deficits, and that this would be a powerful system not only for asking about mechanism but for testing therapies — seeing whether there is benefit before going into clinical trials.

8:12 A very rare neuron type was grown
Aparna Bhaduri at the University of California studies human brain development and cancer. She thinks one highlight of the work is that a cell type differentiated from the human organoids looks like a very rare kind of neuron that has been hard to culture in vitro. Loss of this neuron type is a key factor in a particular dementia, so understanding them better could aid future therapy development. But she also notes there is a long way to go: the cortex's laminar structure and its different processing areas are not well preserved in this system, falling short of being more like a human brain; and the authors themselves state that the developmental stage the organoids reach is still mid-development — this is not a fully mature cortex.

9:12 This is not a human brain in a mouse's head
Asked whether these animals count as human-mouse chimeras, Aparna Bhaduri says plainly: this is not a human brain inside a mouse. There are three reasons — it is immature; the complexity of cell types is insufficient, some cell types are still missing and the ones present are not mature; and although there are some connections with the rodent, the degree and the way they are wired differ from a human brain. So on complexity, maturity and connectivity, she sees this as an organoid pushed forward in its development, not a human brain. Other researchers Nature spoke to agree: these are not fully formed functional human cortex.

10:13 Ethicists are not a stumbling block for scientists
Emily Jackson at the London School of Economics studies the regulation of stem-cell-related research, including brain organoids. She says the most striking thing about this paper, and about the work of Sergio Pasca's lab, is the team's focus on the importance of ethics and regulation. She thinks people sometimes mistakenly treat regulation as an obstacle to scientists, and that this is a genuine error: in her experience, scientists at the frontier of biotechnology very much want ethicists involved, very much want to know where the red lines are, so that they can proceed in the confidence that society approves. She also stresses that when you replace part of a rodent's brain with human brain cells, the key question is what harm this does to the animal — especially a new kind of harm you would not easily notice — and that this must be taken very seriously.

17:19 Turning a paper into an agent you can talk to
James's team at Stanford proposes turning static papers into "knowledge agents" — think of them as a paper's virtual corresponding author. Their workflow is called paper to agent: a set of AI agents reads the paper through, works out how it was done, reproduces the original results, then stores the knowledge in a server that acts as a translation layer between the human paper and any AI, turning models like ChatGPT and Claude into virtual co-authors you can ask anything about the paper, or even run analyses with your own data. James stresses this differs from simply throwing the paper into a chatbot: the latter only reads, interprets and summarises results, does not know how the results and figures were generated, and cannot use the data and code, because it has no hands-on experience; a paper agent has that hands-on experience.

item.title: The Mess in AI Evaluation Isn't a Technical Problem, It's a Transparency Problem
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-nejmaigrandrou-ai-评估的混乱不是技术问题-是透明度问题/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-nejmaigrandrou-ai-评估的混乱不是技术问题-是透明度问题/
item.description: In that 2019 systematic review, fewer than 5% of medical imaging AI papers met the rigor standards long established in other areas of medicine, and even the best-performing models only matched radiologists.
item.content:encoded:
In that 2019 systematic review, fewer than 5% of medical imaging AI papers met the rigor standards long established in other areas of medicine, and even the best-performing models only matched radiologists.

This episode has medium information density, but the first half — a first-hand account of how evidence standards in medical AI moved from chaos to discipline — is directly useful to anyone building medical AI products.

11:22 Fewer than 5% of AI papers in top journals hold up
Around 2019, new papers appeared every week claiming ‘AI is as good as radiologists’ or ‘AI beats radiologists at pneumonia detection’, but these conclusions contradicted each other. Xiao Liu and her collaborators did something no one was doing at the time: they applied the rigorous standards that the diagnostic test evaluation field had used for years to these AI papers, keeping only those with external validation, like-for-like comparisons, and meaningful control groups. The paper count was cut down sharply — fewer than 5% truly met the standards long established in other areas of medicine. And within that small set, the best models only matched radiologists. This isn't bad news; it means there's too much noise in the published literature.

16:28 Reporting guidelines don't teach you how to do research, they force you to say what you did
CONSORT, SPIRIT, PRISMA, STARD, TRIPOD — these reporting guidelines are essentially checklists specifying which items a paper must report. They don't tell you how to do the research — they're not methodology guidelines, they're transparency guidelines. Whether your methods are good or bad, you have to write them transparently and clearly. Their function is to put authors, journal editors, and peer reviewers on the same information plane, with no smoke bombs, no hiding behind vague details. Xiao Liu added a side effect: when authors know they must report a certain item, it反过来 forces methodological rigor to rise, though that's hard to measure.

18:33 Guidelines are produced by Delphi voting; items without consensus get cut
CONSORT AI and SPIRIT AI weren't written by a few people behind closed doors; they went through a Delphi process: first a set of candidate items proposed through literature review and expert opinion, then multiple rounds of multi-stakeholder voting, ending with an in-person discussion. That in-person discussion is often the most valuable, because people learn from each other. Items that fail to reach consensus are excluded; only those that do are kept. Xiao Liu says doing this kind of consensus project properly takes at least six months; she tried a compressed three-month version, but participants contribute their time for free, and to get high-quality feedback and multiple rounds of participation, you can't cut corners on time or reach.

20:36 Whether explainability belongs in reporting guidelines was fought over at the meeting
Andy Beam recalls that one question in the Delphi discussion was: should clinical trials include explainability requirements, or at least report any explainability evaluations you did. He and Lauren Oakden-Rayner stood up on the small stage and said ‘No, it shouldn't be done at all, for the following reasons’. That debate was later commissioned into a paper by Rupa, an editor at Lancet Digital Health, and became one of Andy's most cited papers. Xiao Liu also clearly sides with ‘no’ in the lightning round: she thinks you should first ask why you want AI explainability, and keep asking until you reach the bottom — what you ultimately want is just beneficial effects.

26:43 Being a regulatory consultant without ever working in industry felt insincere
At the time, Xiao Liu was doing academic AI research and clinical ophthalmology while increasingly consulting for regulators. She began to feel she had never stood on the side being regulated, and that consulting was a bit insincere. So she joined Apple as a health scientist, mainly designing validation studies for wearable device algorithms, such as Apple Watch sensing algorithms, including a hypertension notification feature released this year. She says Apple has a well-oiled product shipping machine, which was exactly the experience she wanted. After more than a year there, she returned to Birmingham to build a lab full-time, and then joined Microsoft AI's newly formed medical frontier LLM team.

32:49 Short term, computer scientists set direction; long term, clinicians gatekeep
Asked whether medical AI will be driven more by computer scientists or clinicians, Xiao Liu first asked what ‘driven’ means, and after confirming it means ‘changed’, gave her judgment: short term, computer scientists and engineers; long term, clinicians. The mechanism: the people who process data, choose metrics, and choose benchmarks determine which direction progress goes in the short term; but if the endpoint is truly being used on patients, clinicians will play the gatekeeper role at a later stage.

33:50 Doctors' work won't change much in five years, but should in ten
Xiao Liu thinks doctors' work won't look dramatically different within five years, but very likely will in ten years and beyond, and she hopes it will. The path she envisions: if medical intelligence and models continue advancing at the current pace, the medical profession no longer has to be about accumulating knowledge, or even about the kind of medical reasoning taught in medical school; the focus shifts to being ‘a companion to experience’ — accompanying deteriorating health, sudden health events, daily wellbeing fluctuations, life-changing diagnoses, treatment failures and complications, and perhaps recovery, perhaps not. She thinks people will continuously need something deeply interpersonal on this journey: someone who can call on knowledge but doesn't necessarily carry it themselves, instead translating it into human language.

40:00 The most optimistic thing is dismantling old medical concepts; the most pessimistic is that we dare not
Xiao Liu says she is more optimistic than pessimistic. What excites her most is that aggregating all the knowledge in the medical world might reveal that our understanding of biomarkers, disease phenotype clustering, and existing medical knowledge frameworks is off. She gives her PhD research on inflammatory eye diseases as an example: a bunch of diseases are loosely called ‘white dot syndromes’ just because they produce white dots in the fundus, but they are likely driven by completely different mechanisms. She hopes one way new intelligence emerges is by dismantling these old concepts in medicine. The pessimistic side: this field is inherently cautious, and may resist such dismantling out of unfamiliarity, sticking rigidly to the evaluation methods and guidelines of the past ten or twenty years during a period of new technological change, missing the chance for discovery.

item.title: He Treated Cancer With Bacterial Toxins and Was Dismissed by His Peers for Forty Years
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-stuffmissed-他用细菌毒素治癌症-被同行骂了四十年/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-stuffmissed-他用细菌毒素治癌症-被同行骂了四十年/
item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: Coley used streptococcal toxins to make tumors vanish in some sarcoma patients, but he couldn't standardize it or explain the mechanism, and radiation and regulation pushed it out; his daughter spent the second half of her life building a cancer research institute around the therapy.
item.content:encoded:
Coley used streptococcal toxins to make tumors vanish in some sarcoma patients, but he couldn't standardize it or explain the mechanism, and radiation and regulation pushed it out; his daughter spent the second half of her life building a cancer research institute around the therapy.

Medium information density: the first half is medical-history background, but the second half — on why the therapy was abandoned and how immunotherapy picked up the thread — is where the value is.

6:13 The death of an 18-year-old patient changed him
In 1890, Coley took on 17-year-old Bessie Dashiell, who had persistent pain after injuring her hand and was eventually diagnosed with periosteal sarcoma. Coley amputated below the elbow, but the tumor soon appeared elsewhere, and she died on January 23, 1891, at just 18 years old, only about 10 weeks after Coley first examined her. Coley was 28, in his first year as a surgeon. Amputation was the only treatment available at the time, and it had not worked, which sent him digging through roughly 90 records of cancer surgery patients at New York Hospital over the previous 15 years, looking for something better.

7:15 In one record, the tumor disappeared on its own
In the case files, Coley found a case from his colleague Dr. William T. Bull: a small round cell sarcoma of the neck that recurred four times, and by the fifth surgery had invaded deep structures and could not be removed. After the operation the patient accidentally developed erysipelas of the face and neck, then had a second attack two weeks later. Within days of the first attack the tumor began to soften and shrank rapidly, and by the time the patient was discharged the tumor had completely disappeared. The hospital had no follow-up records, so Coley went door to door in the German immigrant community and found him: in the spring of 1891 he was still alive, with no local or systemic recurrence, seven years after the surgery.

9:21 He tried live bacteria first, then switched to toxins
On May 2, 1891, Coley began trying to induce erysipelas in a patient with an inoperable sarcoma of the tonsil and neck. The tumor was so large the patient could not eat solid food and could only swallow small amounts of liquid. Coley exposed the patient to bacteria cultured in the lab, but for months could not induce erysipelas, until in October he injected a culture a colleague had brought back from Robert Koch's laboratory in Germany. The patient became very ill, but two weeks later the neck tumor had disappeared and the tonsil tumor had shrunk, and the patient lived in good health for eight years. By the end of 1892, after two early patients died of infection, Coley began working with bacteriologists to heat-kill the bacteria and filter out the toxins, rather than using live bacteria directly.

15:34 The effect was real, but only in a subset of patients
In his papers, Coley wrote that in his own experience, in slightly more than 10% of cases the regression process continued until the tumor was completely absorbed and the patient remained cured; in other cases the improvement was only temporary, and within weeks the tumor regrew and the patient died despite continued injections at higher doses; and in a very small number of cases, especially large, highly vascular tumors, particularly the melanotic type, no clearly beneficial effect was ever observed. By 1909 he was recommending it for all inoperable sarcomas (except the melanotic type), for long-bone sarcomas where surgery meant sacrificing a limb, as prophylaxis against recurrence after surgery for primary sarcoma once the wound had healed, and after surgery for all carcinomas to reduce recurrence using the mixed toxins.

19:40 JAMA withheld judgment, then declared failure two months later
On May 31, 1894, Coley read his paper before the American Surgical Association. In October of that year, JAMA published a piece comparing bacterial toxins to diphtheria antitoxin, saying the best method of use had not yet been determined, that it was still experimental, and calling for patience until experts produced complete results. But only two months later, on December 15, 1894, JAMA published "The Failure of the Erysipelas Toxins," saying "there is no longer much question that the toxin injections have completely failed as a cure for sarcoma and malignant growths," and that although many surgeons had faithfully tried it over the previous six months, not one fully verified recovery had been reported. Coley responded the following January, noting that he had used not only erysipelas toxins but also Bacillus prodigiosus, and that the failure of a few doctors in a limited number of cases would not settle the scientific community's judgment of whether the method succeeded.

23:47 Forty years, a thousand patients, a hundred and fifty papers
Coley worked with these toxins for about 40 years, treated roughly 1,000 cancer patients, and published about 150 papers. In 1909 he wrote that 52 inoperable sarcoma cases had been successfully treated with a mixed toxin of erysipelas and Bacillus prodigiosus, of which 35 remained healthy for 3.25 to 16 years, 28 for 5 to 16 years, and 14 for 10 to 16 years. Although Park, Davis, and Company had been producing various preparations since 1899, the toxins never became the most common treatment for inoperable sarcoma. The reasons included: tense relations with his boss James Ewing, who opposed his research; the bone sarcoma registry refusing to include his cured patients, insisting they had been misdiagnosed; his insistence that all cancers had a microbial origin, even after that idea had been overturned; the difficulty of producing and standardizing the toxins; and the 1902 Biologics Control Act, which raised the regulatory cost.

26:54 Radiation took his window of time
Coley's own method of use was also fairly loose: different patients received different doses by different methods for different lengths of time. Partly this was because he was trying to figure out what worked and how best to do it, but some treatment decisions were made almost on feel rather than data. He also noted that other doctors using his toxins treated patients for much longer than he did, conceding that his own shorter courses might explain some patients' recurrences. X-rays were discovered in 1895 and radium in 1898, and radiation quickly became the standard treatment for many inoperable cancers. Both discoveries came early in his writing about the therapy. In 1934, JAMA published a statement from its Council on Pharmacy and Chemistry that was slightly more positive in wording than 40 years earlier, saying the mixed toxins of erysipelas and prodigiosus might sometimes play an important role in preventing or delaying malignant recurrence or metastasis, and might occasionally cure hopeless inoperable tumors. But by then Coley had already retired, and he died on April 16, 1936, at the age of 74.

29:00 His daughter spent her life building an institute for her father
After Coley died, his daughter Helen Coley Nauts began organizing his papers and correspondence, intending to write a biography, and ended up digging deep into his work. She had no medical qualifications and no formal education beyond high school, but she carefully combed through all of her father's publications, trying to work out what made the difference between success and failure. In 1953, she partnered with philanthropist Oliver R. Gray Sr. to found the Cancer Research Institute, with funding from sources including Nelson Rockefeller. She served as its director until her death in 2001. Her brother Bradley was also an advocate of their father's method, becoming chief of bone surgery at Memorial Hospital after their father retired. Today the Cancer Research Institute has an award named after Coley, recognizing outstanding research in basic and tumor immunology.

item.title: Government Doesn't Just Waste Your Money — It Wastes an Hour of Your Week
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-tyler-政府不只浪费你的钱-还浪费你每周一小时/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-tyler-政府不只浪费你的钱-还浪费你每周一小时/
item.description: Plenty of countries file taxes for their citizens; the IRS is legally barred from doing it for you. The time tax hits the poor, immigrants and the formerly incarcerated hardest — and AI may not save them.
item.content:encoded:
Plenty of countries file taxes for their citizens; the IRS is legally barred from doing it for you. The time tax hits the poor, immigrants and the formerly incarcerated hardest — and AI may not save them.

Medium information density, but the "time tax" frame itself is valuable: it reprices the administrative friction of the welfare state as a regressive levy. The confession in the back half about a shifting UBI stance is worth hearing.

0:58 The IRS is legally barred from filing your taxes for you
Lowrey's core example: in Japan, salaried workers never touch the tax process at all; many countries send you a pre-filled return and you just correct the errors. The US could easily do this — nine in ten households take the standard deduction, and their tax situations are fairly simple — but the IRS is not legally permitted to. This is not a technology problem, it is an institutional choice. She defines the "time tax" as the portion of cost the government shifts onto individuals as administrative labour, and unlike a monetary tax it works differently: you can earn more money, you cannot earn more time.

1:02 The worst program is TANF, not the IRS
Lowrey names TANF (cash welfare) the single worst program in government: it nominally exists to address child poverty, in practice it does not move the child poverty rate, its compliance burden is extremely heavy and punitive, and its $16.5 billion a year is essentially wasted. She offers a rule — programs aimed at high-income Americans are a far better experience, safety-net programs are generally bad, and welfare is the worst. That yields a counterintuitive judgment: the quality of government service is inversely proportional to the political power of the beneficiary.

6:08 Pandemic fraud is not something the time tax can prevent
Cowen raises a common objection: fraud exploded after deregulation in 2020, so maybe the time tax is the necessary cost of fraud prevention. Lowrey rejects it outright: that fraud came mainly from criminal rings and fake small businesses, and from the fact that UI systems themselves run on ancient COBOL infrastructure. Her mechanism is misaligned incentives — governors have no incentive to upgrade UI systems when unemployment is low, so the same conversation repeats every recession. The conclusion: building state capacity and agile digital systems prevents fraud; pushing the work onto individuals does not.

11:19 Large-scale fraud is almost entirely on the supply side
Lowrey points out that Medicare and Medicaid fraud is almost entirely on the provider side: nursing homes, clinics and hospital systems defrauding the government. The ceiling on individual fraud is low, because the money you can extract from the government is limited; to commit large-scale fraud you have to process a lot of transactions. So her policy ordering is: reduce administrative overhead in other programs, concentrate enforcement resources on criminal organisations and legitimate providers, rather than loading burdens onto the 99.9% who do not commit fraud. She adds a piece of political economy: fraud narratives are often used to make programs look illegitimate, so voters tolerate cuts.

13:25 Fifty hours per person per year, and highly unequal
Lowrey's quantitative estimate comes from the American Time Use Survey: total bureaucratic time is about 50 hours per person per year, close to an hour a week. She concedes the number is understated — ATUS cannot capture multitasking (cooking while on hold only gets recorded as one thing), and time taxes are scattered across categories and never totalled. Who pays the most? People entangled with the criminal justice system, immigrants, the poor. The rich can "skip" it with staff and accountants — with one exception: permits to renovate a house in San Francisco, where no amount of money spares you a 500-day wait and multiple rounds of public review.

22:57 AI can fill out forms, but it can't fill a urine test
Cowen asks whether AI agents could handle all of this within five years. Lowrey says probably, but raises two caveats: first, the users of the most burdensome programs are low-income, and whether they know about or trust these agents is an open question; second, much of the burden is not paperwork at all — it is mandatory interviews, urine screening, data that is hard to collect. She gives SNAP as an example: benefits are calculated by household, and the government has no stable definition of "household", so you have to explain how you split staple food costs with the people you live with — a question AI would struggle to answer for you too. She notes she was originally sceptical, but a civic technologist who has worked in this field for years firmly believes AI will help a great deal.

31:18 Disability insurance is already hard enough to apply for
Cowen presses with data: the number of people on disability insurance rose roughly fourfold between 1990 and 2014, while workplace deaths kept falling — shouldn't the bar be raised? Lowrey does not accept the inference. She offers two alternative explanations: population ageing and rising obesity-related chronic illness. Then the counter-evidence: 5% of applicants have to submit more than 1,000 pages of medical material; 11,000 Americans die each year while waiting for a disability determination. She concedes she worries about both directions — about paying people who do not need it, and about rejecting people who genuinely do — so she does not think this is the moment to add more paperwork.

38:28 The research moved her off her UBI position
Lowrey's previous book, Give People Money, was pro-UBI; here she says plainly that the research findings are "sobering", and that she has updated her priors: the side benefits she expected cash to deliver did not materialise. Her defence is that the point of giving people money is to give people money to buy things, and that rationale still holds; improvements in life being smaller than expected is not an argument against the policy. On AI and UBI, she admits she was extremely dismissive back then of the claim that "AI will force UBI", and would not go that far now — but if GDP and productivity surge while unemployment rises at the same time, that would be very strange, and you would have to start considering UBI-type policies.

item.title: After Tome Hit 25 Million Users, He Tore It Down to Build a CRM
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-a16z-tome-做到-2500-万用户后-他推倒重来去做-crm/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-a16z-tome-做到-2500-万用户后-他推倒重来去做-crm/
item.description: Keith Perez walked away from Tome and its 25 million users because his own team didn't like the product; he bets the CRM is won not by making salespeople do more work, but by whether you can fully model a company's customer reality.
item.content:encoded:
Keith Perez walked away from Tome and its 25 million users because his own team didn't like the product; he bets the CRM is won not by making salespeople do more work, but by whether you can fully model a company's customer reality.

The first half is a rare post-mortem on deliberately shutting down a growing product; the second half is dense with operational detail on pricing, expansion and org design.

3:01 They killed a hit not because of the data, but because they didn't like it
Tome launched alongside ChatGPT and reached 2 million users a month, so many that inference capacity ran short and people had to queue. But Keith says what actually made them stop wasn't a metric — it was that "none of us liked the product." Concretely: they couldn't see a path where a discerning, high-quality presentation maker would treat Tome as indispensable, nor one where investment banking or consulting people would write memos in it. Their conclusion was that what the models lacked wasn't general reasoning ability but context about who the presenter is, who the audience is, and what relationship holds between them — and that gap wouldn't close just by waiting for stronger models.

6:04 Follow the heat first, then discover the real problem is data
The Tome team dug through their own user base and found B2B users clustered in sales and marketing, so they ran free pilots with 12 large companies. The original goal was helping sales build new-business decks and proposals, but customers started asking: can you also do research, help us qualify leads, help us understand which companies are worth expanding into. They followed that pull, asking customers to open up access to CRM, call recordings and data warehouses, and found the hardest part wasn't doing that work — it was that the data in those systems contradicted itself. The reality in call recordings and the reality in the CRM often didn't line up. Keith says reorganizing that data started to look like the most important work, so they concluded: if you can reorganize a company's reality into something both machines and people understand, that's more worth doing than the original path.

8:11 Nobody wants your four-month-old CRM, so pay them to use it
What they built first was a go-to-market assistant that AEs used every day, but they couldn't charge for it — the data wasn't theirs, and ten other companies were chasing the same thing. So they cut headcount, rethought the CRM from scratch, worked in stealth for four months, and then found nobody wanted a four-month-old CRM. The only asset left was a huge office lease they couldn't get out of, so they posted on X and LinkedIn: use our CRM and we'll let you sit in our office for free. That's "negative pricing." The 10 startups they brought in were there every day, complaining about slowness and missing features, but giving feedback in Slack every two hours. Keith says this was the exact opposite of Tome: a barely working product that users were inside every day, and that they cared about enough to give feedback by the hour.

11:21 The core of a CRM is relationships, not fields
Three of Lightfield's five founders came from Facebook. Their plain-spoken judgment was that the most important thing in a CRM is modeling relationships, so they borrowed directly from the Facebook timeline and built an activity log first — when you first made contact, what you said, what they said back, which meetings happened, which documents went back and forth, and eventually what the other side did inside your product and how they paid. Every traditional CRM field update and stage progression is triggered off that log, but underneath there's always a canonical relationship log. They also tried going fully unstructured and found queries too slow — a needle-in-a-haystack problem — and landed on semi-structured: stuff a large amount of unstructured data into the activity log and let the system infer causality from the log.

15:26 Get the data model wrong and sales will never go back and fix it
They interviewed a lot of CRM consultants, asking what they actually do for clients, and found the highest-consequence thing is the data model: set your stages and fields wrong and you can't send sales back in time to fill the data in — it's over. So Lightfield chose to be "schema-less": connect email, drop in a call recording, hook up the data warehouse, and the system assembles the relationship in real time; fields come later. Change your mind and it walks the activity log and backfills. Alex Rampell compressed this into "intelligence is greater than schema," and contrasted it with the old era: back then, to save space, every column in a table had to have a predefined varchar length — name varchar 25 — and now they don't even want a schema.

17:28 Someone used it to find a cutting-edge treatment for an Alzheimer's patient
Because it supported fully arbitrary schemas, custom objects and custom relationships from day one, Lightfield attracted a set of customers with very strange business models. Keith's example is Power: on one side it serves pharma companies, helping them find clinical trial participants; on the other it's a marketplace aggregating patients with hard-to-diagnose conditions and hunting for cutting-edge treatments. They modeled both the B2C and B2B sides in Lightfield, wrote automations to scrape the FDA and clinicaltrials.gov, built a world model of every ongoing clinical trial on earth, and then matched patients to pharma companies. The result: Lightfield actually helped an Alzheimer's patient find a cutting-edge treatment within days.

23:37 Win the founders and engineers first, then wait for the sales VP to come around
Alex points out something often overlooked: the sales VP a greenfield company hires was trained by Salesforce and will say flat out, "I don't use that." Lightfield's design principle is to win first the founders, engineering leads and product leads — the people willing to use frontier technology to understand customers — while making every sales-led capability free for anyone in the company to use. That both helps the company understand what engineering, support and finance are doing and creates real intra-company network effects that make replacement harder. By the time that senior sales VP arrives and finds engineering, finance and support all using it for customer understanding and account scoring, the company pushes him to try it — and that's when they get their opening.

32:00 Pure seat-based and pure consumption pricing both blew up
They tried pure seat-based pricing first; acceptance was decent, but top users consumed 10,000 times what the tail did, which doesn't work long term. Then they tried pure consumption pricing, turning everything into credits, and within three weeks nobody touched any feature — Keith calls it the company's worst three weeks, a pile of signups and no usage. Finally they split it into four kinds of work: everyday CRM work (logging meetings, filling fields, updating tasks) goes into a platform fee or seat fee, because customers don't want to budget annually for "the margin of error on core CRM"; pipeline generation is charged on consumption, because there's alpha there and it turns into revenue; workflow automation is charged separately — say someone requests a demo on your website and Lightfield decides this is a deep tech company that should go to Henry and that one is health tech that should go to Matt; and finally intelligence and prediction, which Keith considers Lightfield's most under-explored part, where customers will pay for the alpha.

item.title: Are bad teeth the number one reason kids go to A&E? The number got misread
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-moreorless-儿童看急诊第一原因是牙-数字被念错了/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-moreorless-儿童看急诊第一原因是牙-数字被念错了/
item.description: A British MP said teeth are the number one reason children go to A&E. The actual figure refers to 5-to-18-year-olds hospitalised for tooth decay — not the same thing, and the decay rate is actually drifting down.
item.content:encoded:
A British MP said teeth are the number one reason children go to A&E. The actual figure refers to 5-to-18-year-olds hospitalised for tooth decay — not the same thing, and the decay rate is actually drifting down.

Four fact-checks strung into one episode, fast-paced with medium information density. The teeth and medicines segments have the most solid numbers; the NEET and P-Doom segments work better as thinking exercises.

1:01 Teeth are the number one reason for A&E — that claim is wrong
Leila Moran, a Liberal Democrat MP and chair of the Health and Social Care Committee, said on Radio 4's The World at One that the number one reason children go to A&E is teeth. Chris Venatza, a consultant in paediatric dentistry at Newcastle University, flatly rejected it: she very likely conflated two sets of numbers. What actually ranks first is "hospital admission for tooth decay treatment" — the number one reason 5-to-18-year-olds are admitted to hospital. A&E visits have all sorts of causes, and there is simply no data showing whether dentistry ranks high or low among them. Moran's office later confirmed Chris was right, and that she meant the hospital admission figure, not the A&E figure.

3:09 Lots of hospital tooth extractions, because the rules changed in 2001
When children are hospitalised for teeth, it is usually not for a filling but for an extraction. Extractions are harder for children to bear, so a child who cannot cooperate for an extraction in a dental clinic may need general anaesthetic. There is an institutional turning point here: the rules changed in 2001, and ordinary dental practices were no longer allowed to administer general anaesthetic, so anyone needing it had to go to hospital. So a large share of the hospital admission figures are general-anaesthetic extractions. This explains why "hospital admission" and "A&E" are two entirely different measures — one is a surgical arrangement pushed into hospitals by the rules, the other is an unplanned visit.

4:10 The admission rate is actually falling, not a crisis
Chris gave the admission rate per 100,000 population: about 320 in 2015, down to 270 before the pandemic, and 250 now. Host Tim Harford's reaction was "this doesn't look like a crisis, the trend is even rather encouraging." Chris acknowledged that a pre-pandemic decline is a good thing, but stressed that even so, large numbers of children are still having general anaesthetics and dental treatment in hospital, which is not good in itself. He added one more thing: over the past decade, dental causes have consistently been the number one reason for hospital admission, unchanged for ten years — so the "number one" position is stable, but the absolute level is heading down.

5:10 To see the decay rate, look at school surveys, not admissions
Chris said that to understand the real state of children's tooth decay, there is a better dataset: the government sends dentists into schools to examine five-year-olds. The latest survey found 22% of five-year-olds already have decay reaching the dentine layer — close to a quarter. He said that a quarter of the population having a disease that needs treatment is not a good state of affairs. Over time: about 30.9% in 2008, down to 23% in 2017-2018, then a plateau, with the latest survey slightly down again from the 2022 one. Longer-term data comes from a survey run once a decade since 1973: 72% of five-year-olds had decay in 1973, down to 43% in 2003, roughly halved.

8:15 25% of UK medicines come from Israel — off by two orders of magnitude
US ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee said on the Today programme that 25% of the medicines Britain uses come from Israel. Lizzie McNeill checked the latest ONS import data: in 2025 the UK imported £10 million of medicines from Israel, while total UK medicine imports were about £28 billion, so Israel accounts for just 0.04% — one twenty-fifth of 1%, not 25%. She also ruled out several possibilities: active pharmaceutical ingredients come mainly from India and China, and the more upstream raw materials mainly from China; medicines supplied by Israeli companies (the largest being Teva) are mostly not made in Israel but in European plants in Hungary, Croatia and elsewhere. Teva estimates it supplies one in eight generic medicine packs in the UK, equivalent to one ninth of all prescription medicines, but the other Israeli companies are all too small to push the total to 25%.

13:29 Blame Gove for rising NEETs, and Wales dismantles the case
Education Secretary Lucy Powell wrote in The Times that a million young people have been left behind by the education system Michael Gove led. Daisy Christodoulou rebutted with a natural experiment: Wales and Scotland took the opposite path to Gove's reforms. Wales's NEET rate for 16-to-24-year-olds rose from 14% in 2019 to 17% in 2025, while England's rose from 11% to 13% over the same period — similar levels, similar trends, with Wales rising slightly more. If Gove is responsible for England's rise, then Wales must be responsible for Wales's rise, yet the two sides' policies were completely opposite. She said the NEET rate sits on top of too many factors — economic structure, the minimum wage, taxes, regulation — not just education.

17:51 The teen mental health decline is not unique to England
Responding to the criticism that "Gove's reforms increased academic pressure and damaged mental health," Daisy also looked at the WHO's Health Behaviour in School-aged Children survey, which reports England, Scotland and Wales separately. The results show average life satisfaction among teenagers fell in all three places this century (2000 to 2022), but it also fell across Western Europe and many other regions, so it is not specific to England. Then look at the share of 15-year-olds who "like school a lot": about 10% in England, about 9% in Scotland, about 7.5% in Wales — all low, but basically the same across the three. The share of 15-year-olds overwhelmed by academic pressure is high in all three, with no big difference.

19:59 P-Doom is a subjective probability, and nobody can give a model
Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned, warning that Anthropic and OpenAI are irresponsible on AI safety. Anthropic's Evan Hubinger responded on X: he personally thinks the probability that AI kills all of humanity within the next decade is greater than 10%. Alexander Mark Koch, an assistant professor of global risk and resilience at Cambridge, explained that P-Doom is shorthand for "the probability that AI causes human extinction," and that it is almost always one individual's subjective probability estimate. He said the issue is extremely complex: it involves regulatory capacity, system resilience, where large-model capabilities are heading, autonomous weapons and biotech tools, whether AI can self-improve into an exponential loop, funding, rules, what China will do, and disaster scenarios ranging from science fiction to "a rogue state using a large model to learn to make bioweapons."

item.title: Sequoia's Former Boss on Reading People: What Happens Before 14 Sets the Core
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-ilt-红杉前掌门看人-14-岁前发生了什么-内核就定了/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-ilt-红杉前掌门看人-14-岁前发生了什么-内核就定了/
item.description: Digging into his own refugee family's history, he found that the imprint you absorb unconsciously from your parents before you are 12, 13, 14 stays with you for life; what changes afterward is the external intensity, not the core.
item.content:encoded:
Digging into his own refugee family's history, he found that the imprint you absorb unconsciously from your parents before you are 12, 13, 14 stays with you for life; what changes afterward is the external intensity, not the core.

Not an investing lesson but a retrospective on origins, reading people, and writing. The back half — on structural shifts in venture and the great man view of history — is the most valuable; the family history up front is more personal.

7:23 The grandfather who waited for the situation to pass vanished
Moritz's two grandfathers were two responses to the same catastrophe. His maternal grandfather was a lower-court judge in Bavaria, had fought at Verdun in World War I, believed in the durability of the state, and had a pension he was unwilling to give up, so he delayed leaving; in the end he and his wife were sent east and disappeared from history. The other grandfather was nearly blind, supported the family alone by trading cattle, had no pension to wait for, and left with his wife 72 hours before the war broke out — three days later and they too would have died. Moritz says the lesson he draws is not a moral judgment but that you must always have a bolt hole to hide in, and never too many passports.

21:03 His most effective question makes people cry on the spot
When he interviews people he always asks one fixed question: looking back, if there were one thing, one action you could have done differently, what would it be. He remembers a person interviewing at Sequoia bursting into tears when asked — the man was the son of Latino immigrants, had stolen candy from a corner grocery with friends at around 12, the shopkeeper told his father, and his father dragged him back to the store by the ear and made him apologize and empty his pockets. Years later, asked this question, the first thing he thought of was still the shame he had brought on his family. Moritz says many people conducting interviews are not really listening to the answer.

26:03 He sorted everyone he knew on Zoom
Inspired by a series about a French village in World War II, he divides people into three categories: resisters, the silent, and collaborators. During the pandemic, in those Zoom meetings with a dozen little windows, he would stare at each person he knew and think: if these people had lived in a French village in the 1940s, who would stay silent, who would resist, who would collaborate. He says resisters are always a tiny minority, because bad things happen in a country precisely because most people stay silent. Asked how many of the people he has backed would be resisters, he says he would like to think so, but he is not sure.

38:04 The painter gave himself one day off a year
Frank Auerbach was a refugee from Nazi Germany, and Moritz calls him a complete monomaniac: apart from one day off each Christmas at Brighton Pier, he painted every single day. His models were a small fixed group of people, the same few faces painted for decades; one model who lived in Venice flew to London once a week to sit for him. His wife's house sits on the English coast, and Moritz asked whether he went there; he answered: I have never been to that house. From this Moritz discusses the cost of monomania — the cost to relationships is almost inevitable, but sometimes great things come out of exactly there.

43:04 He bet on something beyond the résumé
Around 1985, Moritz was still a journalist and wrote to five small funds looking for a job. Everyone except Don Valentine told him he had no technical background, no engineering degree, no experience at a tech company, and suggested he go into PR or marketing. Don was willing to take the risk, for a direct reason: he had seen several people with operating backgrounds at large tech companies move into investing and fail, and he had also seen several who succeeded — an actuary, and the one he cites most, Arthur Rock: an investment banker by background, with nothing in his résumé that predicted success. Don did not believe in teaching people; he believed in throwing them into the deep end and seeing whether they drowned.

46:15 Venture's old advantage was imperfect information
Moritz says doing venture in the 1980s and 90s had several advantages that have now disappeared, the first being imperfect information: before the internet, unless you were close to something you did not know what was happening, whereas now the whole world basically gets the same information. The second is that the early market has far too many participants — individuals, two- or three-person funds, giant mutual funds — too many intermediaries, and it is no longer possible for investors to build the kind of real, close relationship with founders they once had. He therefore says a moderately smart, mentally agile 14- to 16-year-old could have done venture in the mid-80s; he is not sure he could still do it well today.

52:57 He believes in the great man view of history without apology
Asked whether it is great individuals or enduring institutions that shape the course of history, Moritz's answer is blunt: he is a firm believer in the great man theory. From Lee Iacocca to Steve Jobs, from politics to the battlefield, what matters is great leaders; and of course also tyrants who cast a shadow over tens of millions of people for decades. In his work at Sequoia and in writing Ferguson, he cares about the same thing — how an organization stays alive across decades. And on Elon, he says he is completely stunned by the scale of his achievements across several different industries, and thinks he may be the greatest industrialist in American history.

58:40 The more AI writes, the more a human voice is worth
Moritz says that because AI can easily produce vast amounts of text, excellent writing that cuts through the junk is appreciating in value; his definition of excellent writing is ‘a voice you can hear that cannot be mistaken for anyone else's’. The hardest thing for a writer is to get close enough to his own inner feeling and voice that it outweighs the weight of others' expectations — he quotes Joseph Campbell: the privilege of a lifetime is to become who you truly are, and that is also the hardest thing. He does not consider himself a technologist and says AI is rarely discussed at home; on employment he is optimistic: people predicted doomsday when the atomic bomb exploded, and predicted a genetic revolution creating humans in the 1970s, and neither happened, and this time he thinks more jobs will be created than destroyed.

item.title: The strongest El Niño hasn't peaked yet, but no one alive has seen one this big
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-ologies-最强厄尔尼诺还没到峰值-但没人活着见过它这么大/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-ologies-最强厄尔尼诺还没到峰值-但没人活着见过它这么大/
item.description: The 2026 El Niño already exceeded the peaks of the two strongest events on record, 1982 and 2015, by autumn — and its peak usually doesn't arrive until winter. This is not a climate forecast for the future; it is weather that is happening now.
item.content:encoded:
The 2026 El Niño already exceeded the peaks of the two strongest events on record, 1982 and 2015, by autumn — and its peak usually doesn't arrive until winter. This is not a climate forecast for the future; it is weather that is happening now.

Meteorologist Marshall Shepherd lays out the mechanics of El Niño, how it is observed, and what it actually does — and takes apart how a UN report got misread by the media as a "strategic retreat." High information density, worth listening to.

5:24 The UN didn't say retreat — a reporter said it first
On September 2, 2026, the UN Environment Programme published a report titled "Limiting Overshoot." AP reporter Seth Borenstein wrote "strategic retreat" in the first sentence of his story, and the phrase was copied into headlines worldwide, turning into an end-of-the-world narrative of "we're done for." But the word "retreat" does not appear in the report at all; the UN was in fact doubling down on emissions cuts. What was actually given up was only the claim that 1.5 degrees can still be held. The report's own text says: every fraction of a degree avoided, every year of overshoot shortened, saves lives, protects ecosystems and reduces economic losses.

11:40 Climate change isn't about to knock — it's already at the dinner table
Shepherd says the framing he grew up hearing was "climate change is coming," and that framing is now outdated. In his words, it isn't just sitting at the dinner table — it's eating dessert, the appetizer and all the main courses. He explicitly rejects any narrative that talks about climate change in the future tense: people used to discuss what 2050 or 2100 would look like, but it is already happening, and it will only get worse, because the emissions cuts that should be happening aren't really happening. He also notes that adaptation and resilience measures are increasing, because some places have realized this is bound to happen.

17:50 El Niño is named after fishermen who caught no fish at Christmas
Every two to seven years, the Pacific trade winds weaken or even reverse, warm water in the western Pacific flows back east, and the upwelling of cold water off South America is shut off. Peruvian fishermen found they caught no fish around Christmas — because the nutrients brought up by that cold water were cut off — and so the name El Niño was born. The opposite, cold phase is La Niña. Shepherd stresses that this is a coupled ocean-atmosphere system, so it takes both meteorology and oceanography to understand. El Niño disturbs the upper-level jet stream through "teleconnections," spreading its effects worldwide; California, Georgia, the Amazon and the Sahel are all on that chain.

19:55 No hurricanes in the Atlantic, but Hawaii issued its first-ever tornado warning
El Niño suppresses Atlantic hurricane activity while strengthening the Pacific hurricane season. As of September 8, not a single hurricane had formed in the Atlantic, only a few tropical storms, and it was likely to break the record for the latest first hurricane since 1941. On the other side, Hawaii got the first tornado warning in the state's history because of Hurricane Lowell, with gusts on Kauai reaching 84 miles per hour. Shepherd says this is El Niño's two sets of books: the East Coast benefits, the Pacific islands come under pressure. California, meanwhile, faces strong storms, rain and mudslides.

35:24 Eight degrees of warm water below the surface means there's no turning back this time
The threshold for calling an El Niño is sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific running 0.5 degrees Celsius above average, and right now they are already two to three degrees above. More critical is what lies below the surface — the estimate Shepherd cites is subsurface water temperatures running eight degrees above normal. He says this is what convinced him the 2026-2027 El Niño warming event will not fall back. World Meteorological Organization data show that by February 2027 this El Niño is almost certain to still be holding strong. He stresses that he is not a scientist given to exaggeration, but this may be the strongest El Niño that anyone alive on Earth has ever seen.

38:33 Weather is mood, climate is personality
Shepherd uses this metaphor to explain why every El Niño is different — they have their own "personalities," but the West Coast's average personality is heavy rain and natural disasters like landslides and mudslides. His concrete advice is an "El Niño plan": know where your important documents are, know what extreme weather your area tends to get under El Niño, and know which National Weather Service office covers you — Los Angeles, San Francisco and Sacramento each have their own office issuing warnings. He also mentions the nighttime tornadoes common in the Southeast, and suggests people make checking the weather before bed a habit, like brushing their teeth.

49:17 Teleconnections: how a blob of warm water in the Pacific changes global weather
Shepherd explains that the mechanism by which El Niño affects the globe is called "teleconnection." A large blob of warm water in the central and eastern Pacific changes the atmospheric column above it, disturbing the upper-level jet stream. He uses the analogy of ripples in a pond: drop a few sticks or a stone in the middle of the ripples and they get scrambled. The disturbance El Niño creates propagates through the atmosphere via teleconnection patterns, carrying weather changes around the world. He also stresses that it is precisely because fluid dynamics is governed by physical equations — the Navier-Stokes equations, thermodynamic equations, the continuity equation — that weather is predictable to some degree; forecasting is essentially predicting how this fluid will flow.

56:37 After El Niño comes a fiercer fire season
Shepherd points out that the problem with extreme weather is that "both sets of books go wrong" — it isn't just drier or just wetter, it's both. El Niño brings rain, storms and mudslides to the western US, but it also makes vegetation grow heavily; a year or two later, when the climate turns dry, that vegetation becomes fuel and amplifies fire season. He calls this a Jekyll and Hyde, dual-personality effect, and says it is why he has devoted so much attention to studying the western US. He also mentions that his colleague Kim Cobb has studied whether El Niño is getting stronger or more frequent because of climate change, and believes a link is likely.

item.title: Margin debt hits a record, and retail is trading stocks with borrowed money
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-planetmoney-保证金债务创纪录-散户正在用借来的钱炒股/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-planetmoney-保证金债务创纪录-散户正在用借来的钱炒股/
item.description: Margin debt at US brokerages now exceeds total US credit card debt, and a leveraged ETF crash in Korea forced the liquidation of 360,000 accounts, most of them belonging to people under 35.
item.content:encoded:
Margin debt at US brokerages now exceeds total US credit card debt, and a leveraged ETF crash in Korea forced the liquidation of 360,000 accounts, most of them belonging to people under 35.

A two-part Indicator mashup. The first half on Korea's leverage blowup has concrete mechanics and numbers; the second half on sports betting is thin on information, so you can listen to just the first half.

1:00 Margin debt has passed credit card debt
Total borrowed money in US stocks has hit a record, over $1.5 trillion, up 50% from a year ago. A more intuitive comparison: total margin debt in the US brokerage system now exceeds total US credit card debt. In other words, more money is borrowed to trade stocks than is owed on credit cards. Making money with other people's money is great, until the market falls — the loan and the interest still have to be paid. Yale finance professor Heather Tewks says that when a stock falls too far, investors have only two choices: sell the stock to repay the loan, or put more money into the margin account.

3:03 India gave academics a natural experiment
Heather Tewks and her co-authors chose to study India because Indian regulators designed the rules in a way that is friendly to scholars: there is a clear dividing line between which stocks can be bought on margin and which cannot. This forms a natural experiment to test whether margin trading really causes market instability. The conclusion is yes — margin does play a role, especially during financial crises. On the way down there is an amplification effect: the basket of margin-eligible stocks falls significantly more than the basket of non-margin-eligible stocks. Many margin investors are forced to sell holdings to repay loans, and this forced selling amplifies the overall losses.

4:04 Korea turned leveraged ETFs into a national game
The same mechanism just played out in Korea. Investors piled into SK Hynix and Samsung, the two companies making memory chips for AI data centers that dominate the Korean stock market. Fidelity global macro director Yurian Timmer describes it: semiconductor earnings tripled over the past year, everything felt like it was on fast-forward, a boom-bust cycle amplified across multiple dimensions. Earlier this year Korea legalized single-stock leveraged ETFs — they look like ordinary ETFs on the outside, but inside they hold leverage, futures and various financial tricks to magnify gains, and losses are magnified just the same. Such products have been legal in the US since 2022, and Korea wanted to catch up. On some days these ETFs accounted for 20% of volume on Korean exchanges.

6:05 The fundamentals were fine, and accounts still went to zero
Yurian Timmer's assessment of these tools: ‘I call them weapons of self-destruction, and I don't understand why regulators approve these things.’ His pessimistic call was at least borne out in Korea: the Korean stock market's market cap at one point plunged 40%. At the company level, memory chip demand is still forecast to be strong, but investors were less excited, leveraged bets began to unwind, and margin traders were forced to sell. More than 3% of Korean adults received a margin call. Goldman Sachs estimates that about 360,000 brokerage accounts were forced to liquidate all holdings to repay debt, and Citi data shows most of these accounts belong to people under 35. Yurian's summary: the fundamentals of these companies are perfectly fine, the problem is just that you slid too far forward — with leverage you can lose your entire principal.

7:07 The Fed has a tool it hasn't touched in decades
In the US, margin debt is also at a historic high, and the Fed actually has a little-known duty: setting how much money investors must have in their own pocket to borrow a dollar. Back to the opening example — you have $50 and want to buy $100 of Apple stock, the Fed can say, be careful, the broker can only lend you $25 instead of $50. The Fed fiddled with this requirement in the years after the Great Depression, and that crash came right after margin debt surged and blew up a bubble. But Yurian thinks we are not yet at the panic point: during the 2000 dot-com bubble the rate of change in margin debt was 81%, today it is about 40%, much slower. He calls the current moment a yellow zone, not a panic point. The Fed has not touched this requirement since 1974, and when reporters contacted its press office, no one was willing to respond on the record.

9:13 Spotting a bubble is easy, timing the pop is hard
Yurian Timmer thinks the Fed may be reluctant to intervene in margin trading, for a simple reason: the Fed generally does not want to get mixed up in the stock market and bubbles, they think no one can predict these things. Greenspan called the Nasdaq a bubble back in 1996, and it ran for another four years. So the Fed is at least humble enough to know it cannot time these things. Spotting a bubble forming is easy, timing the pop is much harder — you don't want to shut down a party that might keep going for a long while.

11:16 A quarter of Gen Z treat sports betting as investing
The line between investing and gambling has already blurred. Over the past year, more than half of Gen Z said they used money originally meant for investing to place sports bets. Sports betting ads keep promoting free bets like ‘deposit $5, get $300’, making betting look like easy money. Eight years after the federal sports betting ban was overturned, the impact on young people is only now showing up. In a recent survey, about a quarter of Gen Z said they see sports betting as a high-risk investment strategy, or a way to reach a goal faster. Dan Egan, vice president of behavioral science and investing at Betterment, says the danger is that we start treating a hobby as an investment — like people who collect cars, who honestly admit that is not making money, it is a hobby.

14:28 Colorado chose to add friction for bettors
State governments are starting to respond to the negative effects of sports betting, such as addiction. Colorado passed a new law making it the first state that allows sports betting to ban betting companies from sending customers mobile push notifications and texts — those ‘hey, looks like there's a game, want to bet’ reminders are cut off. The bill also limits the number of deposits a single customer can make in a day, capped at six. Co-sponsor and Democratic state senator Matt Ball says he is not trying to ban gambling — he has bet on sports himself and has been commissioner of a fantasy league for 15 years — but people in his district came to him about the issue, from a mother whose son came home from college and ran up $15,000 on a credit card in one night, to problem gambling experts nationally. Problem gambling is linked to more bankruptcies, loan defaults, domestic violence and suicide. Matt himself admits: we don't have any data, we are guessing to some degree.
