Tobi directly rebuts the third: the occasion where intuition is most valuable is precisely when there is no direct feedback. Because if there are five paths that all look good, and one of them has fast feedback, everyone floods toward it, and that is short-termism. He gives company examples: long-term investment, refactoring, entering a new market, or refusing a new market to go deep in the existing one — none of these have feedback loops; whereas pumping the share price has a daily quote. He says he has found a high correlation between "the right path" and "no feedback loop."

56:23 SpaceX gets there by subtraction, not addition
Tobi says the first-generation Raptor was already a working solution and could have stopped there, but SpaceX kept iterating to the second and third generations. The third looks mostly 3D-printed, whereas the dense plumbing on the first was, at the time, the only way to build that engine — yet by today's manufacturing, every one of those pipes is wrong and doesn't need to exist. His conclusion: you can't make something better and better by piling things on; you have to prune, you have to rebuild, you have to put a period on things. He also says failure itself isn't the problem, unless it's catastrophic, because a product failure frees up a scarcer resource — people with product vision — to go do the next thing.

item.title: In the Short Term, AI Is a Complexity Machine, Not an Efficiency Tool
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-15-masterscale-ai-短期是复杂制造机-不是效率工具/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-15-masterscale-ai-短期是复杂制造机-不是效率工具/
item.description: AI lets anyone write and do research, and the result is more emails, more decks, more decisions. Jim VandeHei says that in the short term it manufactures complexity, and only deliberate deletion buys your time back.
item.content:encoded:
AI lets anyone write and do research, and the result is more emails, more decks, more decisions. Jim VandeHei says that in the short term it manufactures complexity, and only deliberate deletion buys your time back.

Medium information density, but the "confront, delete, amplify" framework and the hands-on details of Axios's homegrown health AI agent are worth the listen.

5:07 Six-month planning is already a fantasy
Jim says he used to mock one-, two-, three-year plans, and now even six-month plans seem laughable to him — he can only have high confidence in things six to seven weeks out. He gives a concrete number: six months ago, 30% to 40% of Axios's traffic came from Google Search; now it's down to 5% to 10%, involving millions of users, and it happened almost overnight. He calls this state post-processable velocity: the AI world is moving faster than humans can understand it. This isn't abstract anxiety — it's a traffic structure rewritten within a few months.

8:07 Most companies are stuck in the messy middle
Jim calls the current phase the messy middle: companies start using AI, build prototypes, see the promise, and then discover "I have to connect this to my data pool," which is far harder than expected. He describes a split: people in Silicon Valley feel like it's 1999 and everything is about to explode; but most people in Toledo, Topeka, Oshkosh feel like "I'm just running my company, AI is probably that new thing, employees are talking about it, we'll get to it eventually." Introducing any technology into an existing company is hard, because you have to wire it into the clunky systems built over the past decade.

9:10 In the short term, AI is a complexity machine
Jim says flat out that for most people, in the short term, AI is a complexity creation machine. The mechanism: now anyone can use AI to write something decent, anyone can do deep research and dump it into an email to their boss. The result is that everyone gets more emails, more decks, more ideas — some well thought out, many not. So it's "oh God, now I have more decisions to make." This is exactly why he wrote the book: how to help you delete the things you do out of habit and inertia, so you can amplify what you actually want to do.

10:16 The 25% wasted each week is habit, not ability
Jim cites data from The Economist and others: on average, 25% of each week is spent on things that shouldn't be done at all, or that have no value to the company, and the cause is habit and inertia. He does the math: 25% means two and a half years wasted out of every decade. He stresses that AI won't solve this right now — "I thought AI would make us more productive; right now it isn't." In the short term people are anxious and confused, and he thinks you should be anxious and confused, because this is a strange time to be alive.

12:21 First confront, then delete, and only then amplify
The framework has three steps: confront is the psychological move, asking "why am I doing this" and "does this meeting really need to happen"; delete is cutting it or saying no; amplify is doing what you're good at, what you enjoy, what brings a promotion or a payoff. Jim says this system has been running at Axios for two or three years, and the effect is that people are more focused and more productive, but most importantly happier. He gives the example of the "let's kill shit" meeting: gather the leadership team, spend an hour or two listing every stupid meeting, process and product, then kill them. That's how the Axios app got cut — tens of millions of people come to Axios, but only 30,000 use the app regularly, while the maintenance cost was extremely high.

15:28 Make more decisions and your decision-making degrades
Jim says the average person receives about 120 texts and 150 emails a day, and this mental strain is underestimated. He cites brain-scan research: the more decisions you make, the worse your ability to make decisions, and this is called cognitive fatigue. So unless you reduce the number of decisions you have to make, you won't perform well on the decisions you actually care about. He gives a personal example: he set recurring purchases like toothpaste and deodorant to Amazon auto-subscribe so he never has to think about them again. Add up these small things and you get fewer decisions and more time — enough to read, to have coffee with someone.

23:45 AI won't replace reporters, it will replace generic consultants
Jim says he doesn't think AI will replace reporters, and doesn't think it will replace most jobs. He names one that will be replaced: the generic consultant — AI is already decent at general consulting and business analysis. But for anyone with passion, as long as they can treat this technology as a force multiplier for their specific work and get very fluent with it, they'll be fine, even more in demand. He judges that fluency with AI will soon become table stakes in the workplace. The logic behind Axios Local's expansion is here too: use AI for distribution, copy editing and other back-end work that isn't core to journalism, drive costs down, then hire hundreds of reporters.

25:47 Never bet your business model on a third party's goodwill
Axios has a content licensing deal with OpenAI. Jim's logic is direct: ChatGPT, Google and Anthropic have already eaten all the public information on the internet, including everything Axios has ever written. So there are only two paths — sue like The New York Times and hope to win, or accept a licensing fee. He judges that Axios can't win a lawsuit, and that its content volume isn't large enough for even a win to be worth the damages. He stresses the difference from BuzzFeed betting on Facebook: this revenue could disappear tomorrow and the company's overall performance wouldn't be affected. His principle: never bet your business model on the generosity of a third party that has no vested interest in your business.

item.title: The More You Try to Be Secure, the Less Secure You Are: Secure Means Being Able to Admit You're Not
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-15-secureattach-越想变安全-越不安全-安全型是能承认自己不安全/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-15-secureattach-越想变安全-越不安全-安全型是能承认自己不安全/
item.description: Secure isn't the absence of anxiety, avoidance and jealousy — it's being a safe container for those feelings. Pushing the insecure parts away means re-enacting, on yourself, the criticism and neglect that made you insecure in the first place.
item.content:encoded:
Secure isn't the absence of anxiety, avoidance and jealousy — it's being a safe container for those feelings. Pushing the insecure parts away means re-enacting, on yourself, the criticism and neglect that made you insecure in the first place.

Medium information density. The first half is conceptual clarification; the second half, on memory reconsolidation and the "lava" mechanism, is where the value is. Suited to people who already have a foundation in attachment theory.

8:12 Pretending to be secure makes you less secure
Franco has observed a popular piece of advice: if you're anxious because someone hasn't texted back, "act like a secure person," don't be anxious. Her judgment is that this inflicts a second injury — "not only do I feel anxious, now I feel ashamed of being anxious." It amounts to re-enacting, on yourself, the criticism, shame and neglect that made you insecure in the first place. Her alternative is to first acknowledge: anxiety is allowed, avoidance is allowed, because "we can only heal the parts of ourselves we're willing to acknowledge."

10:12 The secure are the ones who can most easily admit they're insecure
Sarah draws a key distinction: insecure attachment is a pattern, while anxious, secure and insecure are emotional states — the two can't be equated. From this Franco derives the "paradox of security" — the most secure people are the ones most able to admit and acknowledge that they're insecure. So security doesn't depend on what emotions you feel, but on how you respond to them: the anxious catastrophize ("the fact that I feel this means I'm too much, there's something wrong with me"), the avoidant push it away and redirect, and the secure respond with "it's okay that I'm anxious, what do I need." She defines worth as "treating your internal world as if it matters."

14:14 Feel first, then heal, then act
Franco offers a three-step sequence you can use in the moment: feel, heal, do. She gives her own example — a friendship she cared about, that she was actively maintaining but felt one-sided, where the other person cancelled because of an injury. Of course she wanted to feel only understanding, but what she actually felt was rejected. It was only because she was practicing "sweeping a hand across the day to see where the emotional energy lands" that she noticed the feeling at all. She first sat with it and named it, then told herself "I am loved, I am safe," and only then replied to the other person, "take care of yourself." If you skip that step and go straight to the gracious words, the negative emotion accumulates and eventually distorts the relationship.

20:19 Memory is self-esteem's database, and it can be rewritten
Franco's core mechanism: memory doesn't just record the past, it predicts the future — "I've been abandoned in the past. I think it will happen again." That is attachment style. She cites memory reconsolidation theory: every time you revisit a memory, you can change its emotional valence. The method is to return to the scene of being picked up late or abandoned by your parents, and have your adult self tell your childhood self, "I'm here, you're safe, this doesn't mean there's anything negative about you." Research shows that doing this not only reduces trauma symptoms and raises self-esteem, but produces changes in the hippocampus. Sarah uses the metaphor of a blueprint: this is pulling up the original blueprint and editing it.

23:20 Your insecurity is actually trying to protect you
Why is rewriting the blueprint the precondition? Franco's explanation: for an anxious person who expects to be abandoned, letting your guard down, letting yourself feel good, actually receiving the other person's love, is threatening — because if you really are abandoned, you'll be shattered even more thoroughly. So "our insecurities are really trying to protect us." This also explains why simply telling someone to "act secure" often doesn't work: without addressing the memory first, security itself is a threat. Sarah adds: some people are in fact already in a safer environment, but the old blueprint keeps them from seeing it.

26:23 Finding secure relationships is about initiating and discerning
Franco gives two things. The first is initiation: people who believe friendship happens naturally are lonelier over the long run, because they don't put in the effort; you have to show up repeatedly in front of the same group of people, using the mere exposure effect (familiarity breeds liking) — for example, don't just go to one happy hour, sign up for a moms' group. At the same time you have to overcome covert avoidance — being there in body but not in mind, scrolling your phone or only talking to people you already know. The second is discernment: ask yourself what your nervous system feels like around this person, whether you're calm, whether there's reciprocity, whether your values are similar, whether the other person genuinely wants you to succeed. She also mentions mutuality: holding your reality and my reality at the same time.

29:25 Reflective functioning determines whether attachment passes to your child
Sarah introduces reflective functioning: the capacity to notice and be curious about your own and others' internal states. She says research shows that if you're insecurely attached, your child has a 70% chance of having the same style; and among the portion who don't pass it on, one predictor is how high their reflective functioning is. Franco sees this as consistent with the mechanism described earlier — only once you can perceive your own internal world do you have the spare capacity to recognize another person's world, because you're less in a threatened state.

33:25 "I was perfectly agreeable" may be a signal of numbness
Franco interviewed a numb interviewee and asked what the signs of numbness were; the answer was "I was perfectly agreeable." This woman saved her dark side for her child — because a child won't leave, she no longer had to maintain connection by being agreeable, and she had even once locked her daughter out of the house, which she felt deeply ashamed of. From this Franco rewrote her own definition of a good person: a good person isn't someone who never feels negative emotions, but someone who allows themselves to feel them — otherwise the emotions accumulate and eventually hijack you at some moment, hurting someone more vulnerable than you. She also notes that internalizers turn emotions on themselves, showing up as depression and persistent anxiety.

item.title: He Dumped an Entire Font into the Thames So No One Else Could Use It
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-15-ninepi-他把整套铅字倒进泰晤士河-只为没人能用它/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-15-ninepi-他把整套铅字倒进泰晤士河-只为没人能用它/
item.description: Over 173 nights, Thomas Cobden-Sanderson dumped 2,600 pounds of Doves Type into the Thames, because metal type is a physical object — dump it and you own it exclusively.
item.content:encoded:
Over 173 nights, Thomas Cobden-Sanderson dumped 2,600 pounds of Doves Type into the Thames, because metal type is a physical object — dump it and you own it exclusively.

A narrative episode about a typeface, a broken friendship and revenge. Not information-dense, but the story itself is extraordinarily vivid — good for a commute.

0:00 Font stories always set listeners off
Roman Mars opens by saying 99PI has done stories about architecture, transit, history and even sports, but stories about fonts and type always draw a huge response from intensely passionate listeners. This episode came out of a segment Helen Zaltzman and Martin Austwick developed for the live stage show Souvenirs, later adapted for radio.

5:20 Friends who live too close fall apart faster
Emery lived at 3 Hammersmith Terrace; in 1897 the Thomas family moved to number 7 on the same street, and Emery even rented commercial space from Thomas. The two took family holidays together and stayed in neighboring cottages. In 1899 they decided to go further and start Doves Press as partners. Helen says they had been very important friends for more than a decade, but the relationship fell apart in only about two years.

9:41 Complementary skills couldn't save the partnership
Thomas was the perfectionist who cared only about the art of printing; Emery was the pragmatist who ran the business. On paper it was a perfect match, but things soured almost from the start. Thomas felt he did all the printing and proofreading himself, that Emery was hardly ever there, and that Emery never responded to his long arguments about how the letter of should be designed. Emery, meanwhile, had another business to run and money to make, and had no time to spend weeks or months with Thomas fussing over a single letter.

13:47 Type is a physical object, so ownership can be fought over
The breakup dragged on for seven years, and the core issue was who owned Doves Type. At the time a typeface was thousands upon thousands of physical objects that couldn't be copied infinitely — without that set of metal type, you didn't have that typeface. Thomas wanted it exclusively and didn't want Emery, or anyone else he couldn't control, printing anything in Doves. He offered a small sum for Emery to give up his rights; Emery wouldn't accept, and the back-and-forth went on for years.

15:58 Dumping it in the river was a revenge seven years in the planning
Thomas throwing Doves Type into the Thames was not a sudden impulse. He waited seven years and wrote a 116-page apologia — the word doesn't mean an apology, it means a defense. He had wanted to publish it in 1913, but realized it might incriminate him, so he kept waiting, until he was about to shut down Doves Press and print its last book, and only then, on an evening in August 1916, did he act.

18:11 173 nights, no more than 15 pounds at a time
Thomas could carry at most 10 to 15 pounds of type at a time, and the full set weighed at least 2,600 pounds. By that math he made at least 173 trips to the bridge. Each night he wrapped the type from the page he had just printed in white paper, bagged it, stuffed it into his pockets or into a wooden toolbox with a sliding lid, and sprinkled it gently off the bridge — he didn't want a splash, and he didn't want to be seen. He was afraid of being caught, because the type had legally been promised to Emery.

24:24 Nearly a hundred years later, someone found it on the riverbed
Emery had asked the original engraver, Edward Prince, to remake Doves Type, but Prince was nearly eighty and his eyes and hands could no longer do such fine work. Then in 2010 the type designer Robert Green began redrawing it. He spent three years making a digital version, wasn't satisfied, and in 2014 went himself to the exposed riverbed under Hammersmith Bridge at low tide, where within 20 minutes he found a lowercase v; he later brought in a dive team and together they found 151 pieces of Doves Type.

33:46 Whoever leaves more writing controls the narrative
Helen says Thomas left behind a huge number of letters and diaries, while Emery's letters are far fewer, so Thomas had a stronger grip on the narrative. For decades people assumed Emery was the jerk, because he complained less. In the diaries of his last forty years, Thomas edited Emery out entirely, and when Annie published those diaries on the fourth anniversary of his death, Emery wasn't in them.

item.title: Renaissance Doctors Came in Four Tiers, and the Best Healer Was Called a Quack
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-15-tpwky-文艺复兴的医生分四等-最会治病的却被叫庸医/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-15-tpwky-文艺复兴的医生分四等-最会治病的却被叫庸医/
item.description: Bone-setters worked the market circuit every week, far more practiced than a licensed surgeon who did a few cases a year, and the physicians called them quacks — title and skill were never the same thing.
item.content:encoded:
Bone-setters worked the market circuit every week, far more practiced than a licensed surgeon who did a few cases a year, and the physicians called them quacks — title and skill were never the same thing.

A medical history interview, medium information density. The most valuable parts are the stratification of the medical marketplace, the origins of credential monopoly, and the era when bloodletting, purging and vomiting were enshrined as the three great therapies.

10:55 Eighty to ninety percent of medical care was provided free by women
Erin asks who was practicing medicine in this period, and Alanna Skuse's answer is ‘almost everyone’ — but the real base of supply was women: household healers carried roughly 80%, perhaps 90%, of medical care, and most of it was charged very little or nothing at all. The reason they were overlooked by history is concrete — they left too little written material behind. Knowledge passed down the maternal line: mother to daughter, aunt to niece, sometimes mistress to servant, carried in handwritten recipe books. They also wrote to each other exchanging ‘I found a good recipe’ and ‘I tried this and it didn't work.’ This formed a medical network with no licenses, no college, and yet coverage of the vast majority of the population.

17:11 See the wallet before the patient: ten shillings a visit
The path to care was essentially a price ladder. At the very top was the physician, about 10 shillings a visit, extremely expensive, so only the wealthy called a doctor directly. Those without money worked upward from the bottom: first a local woman, a midwife with extra medical knowledge, or a nearby gentlewoman with leisure and literacy; failing that, an apothecary, whose medicines started at a penny, like today's pharmacist, except nearly every one sold his own special remedies and sometimes examined and diagnosed patients himself; failing that, or with an obviously broken leg, a surgeon, about 3 shillings a visit, handling everything on the body's surface — lumps, wounds, fractures. Skuse states plainly that how sick you let yourself get before seeking care depended on what it cost: ‘the doctor or dinner.’

28:23 The guild monopoly failed, but the idea of credentials stayed
Skuse characterizes the motive behind the founding of the College of Physicians as straightforwardly commercial: physicians resented surgeons and barber-surgeons encroaching on their turf and wanted to build a college and then monopolize all medical practice. The college was built, the monopoly was not obtained — it could not even control London, let alone the country. But the long-term consequence matters more than the short-term outcome: this was the first time the idea that ‘practitioners ought to be credentialed’ took systematic form. Skuse pulls this thread to the present at the end: these institutions, initially weak regulators, evolved into bodies like the British Medical Association and the AMA, and our assumption today that doctors share uniform standards and a consistent opinion starts here.

29:26 Colleagues calling each other quacks was the norm, not the exception
Asked how fierce competition was among doctors, Skuse says they were ‘horribly rude to each other,’ and finding two who did not quarrel was rarer — because there was only one pie and everyone wanted the biggest slice. So surgeons insulted apothecaries, physicians insulted surgeons, and everyone at once called everyone else a quack. She gives an example: someone claimed a certain doctor had gone off to exorcise a woman, when in fact she merely had gas. Quack comes from the Dutch quacksalver, meaning someone who sells salves by boasting of his medical credentials; another word, mountebank, comes from Italian, meaning someone who climbs onto a stage to hawk cures. The key point is that the word's boundary was filthy: a bone-setter would be called a quack by a physician, because he had no credentials and no fixed shop.

31:28 Bone-setters were more practiced than licensed surgeons
This is the sharpest passage in the whole piece. Skuse asks: if you had a complex fracture, would you go to a licensed surgeon who does a few cases a year, or a bone-setter who travels a different market every week and does nothing but set bones? Bone-setters usually also pulled teeth — teeth rotted badly in that era and there was no remedy but extraction — so they tended to be physically strong, and they brought an equally strong assistant to hold the patient down during the procedure. Physicians classed these people as quacks, on the grounds of no credentials and no shop. But by actual surgical volume, their skill far exceeded that of their licensed peers. Credentials and competence here are two independent axes.

36:45 Efficacy was not the main source of trust
Erin asks directly whether efficacy affected trust, and Skuse's answer is: people did not expect to be cured in the first place. They did not expect a life free of pain, nor did they expect a doctor to fix everything wrong with them — but they did judge when a doctor did something wrong. She gives the example of Elizabeth Freke: her husband was gravely ill with a gangrenous leg, she went away for a few days to rest, came back to find him worse, and said outright, ‘you have murdered my husband.’ So trust was more commercial: a doctor who gossiped about his patients would lose business; and if a practitioner held on, people would use the same healer for life, even across generations — a midwife's daughter delivering the daughter of the woman her mother had delivered. She also mentions Henry Moore bringing famous physicians and their prescriptions from continental Europe for Lady Anne Conway, when she might have done better with a local doctor.

38:47 Opponents of bloodletting often believed other nonsense too
Skuse concedes that although the vast majority believed in the humors and all bled, there were public dissenters against bloodletting, with George Thomson one of the leading figures of that camp. The problem is that these people often simultaneously believed other quite absurd things, which undermined their own credibility. On the starting point of evidence-based medicine, she says it is hard to answer, because in a sense medicine has always had evidence-based medicine: in the 16th century they were already testing antidotes on condemned criminals, which looks like experiment; the scientific method as we describe it today emerged roughly with the Royal Society, and James Lind's scurvy trial in 1746 was the first clinical trial in the modern sense. What actually helped people was mostly gentle remedies — sage and rosemary gargles, ginger and mint for the stomach — along with symptom relief and narrative medicine: a doctor who sat at the bedside for an hour listening to you might have you sleeping better that night.

46:55 Bloodletting, vomiting and purging were listed as the three great therapies
Asked about the greatest cost of medical progress, Skuse first gives an institutional answer: surgeons, physicians and apothecaries all crossed boundaries, and it was precisely by crossing boundaries that they learned — at the cost of a great many patients dying of mercury, arsenic, useless operations and aggressive purging. Because experimentation was not systematic or organized, the number of victims far exceeded what was necessary. She also gives a more specific, numerical judgment: the College of Physicians called bloodletting, vomiting and purging the three great therapies, and heaven knows how many people already at death's door were pushed through it by these purging treatments. There was also a cost in quality of life — these therapies were extremely unpleasant.

item.title: When your kid starts eating healthy, it may be the start of an eating disorder
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-15-asklisa-孩子开始吃得健康-可能是进食障碍的起点/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-15-asklisa-孩子开始吃得健康-可能是进食障碍的起点/
item.category: Ask Lisa: The Psychology of Raising Tweens & Teens
item.description: Eating disorders survive on secrecy, so when parents see the first signs they should say it out loud. Your kid won't get worse — she may actually feel relief, because someone finally made the decision for her.
item.content:encoded:
Eating disorders survive on secrecy, so when parents see the first signs they should say it out loud. Your kid won't get worse — she may actually feel relief, because someone finally made the decision for her.

Medium information density, but the notice-ask-act framework and the "don't walk on eggshells" stance are directly actionable for parents.

6:11 The more alert the parent, the safer the child
Bhatnagar says that when a parent says "something feels off" and actively seeks out a specialist, that itself is a protective factor. She frames it as a "worry column" and a "reassurance column": a child falling off the growth curve or losing weight goes in the worry column; a parent who is observing, asking questions, staying curious — rather than saying "oh, she's eating healthy, great" — goes in the reassurance column. She stresses that adolescents generally should not be losing weight, and falling off their own growth arc is a "telltale sign" — it warrants further evaluation.

12:28 Eating disorders thrive off of secrecy
Bhatnagar says "eating disorders thrive off of secrecy," and breaking the silence is the first step of intervention. She describes a scene common in clinic: a kid walks in wearing baggy leggings and says, "Dr. B, I think you're crazy, I'm completely fine." There is a huge gap between what the parent sees and what the child experiences. So parents shouldn't be afraid of making their kid angry — an angry reaction is very common, but afterward the child often feels relief, because someone finally made the decision for her.

14:29 Don't walk on eggshells — rock the boat
Lisa sums it up: parents are afraid of upsetting their kid, so they don't dare bring it up. Bhatnagar's position is "go ahead and rock the boat" — but with care about how you rock it. She gives the NAA framework: Notice (watch for changes beyond weight — mood, social life, schoolwork), Ask (ask with curiosity and empathy, not accusation; accusation inevitably builds a wall of defensiveness), Act (you don't have to wait for the child to agree or admit there's a problem before acting — just book the professional evaluation).

17:30 An ordinary pediatrician may miss it
Lisa says she has seen this in her own clinical work: she refers a child she's very worried about to a pediatrician, and the pediatrician says "she's fine, she's doing great," while Lisa is thinking "I really don't think so." That slows the whole process down. Bhatnagar agrees — find someone with specialized training to do the evaluation, because eating disorders span physiological, emotional and psychological domains, and evidence-based treatments now exist, so finding the right person directly determines the outcome. The first-line standard treatment for adolescent anorexia is Maudsley family-based treatment (FBT).

20:38 Ninety percent of kids start with "I want to be healthy"
Bhatnagar says that among the kids she treats, 90% of the problems began with "I want to start eating healthy" — not an intentional slide into an eating disorder, but health class taught them how to take care of their body, and then they started changing things. Some kids are completely fine, but not all of them. So parents should join with them, while curiously asking "what does this mean to you," and confirm the child isn't going to extremes, because "what you learn on TikTok isn't always healthy." If these efforts look unhealthy, you still have to act.

22:47 Intervene before it's etched into the brain
Lisa uses a drug analogy: if a kid tries marijuana for a few weeks, turning around isn't hard; three years in, it's a completely different situation. Eating is the same — intervene when the random dieting has just started and you can change things quickly; once it's gone far, it's much harder. Bhatnagar agrees completely, saying you want to step in before the illness is "fully entrenched in the brain." She explains what being etched into the brain means: the child can no longer separate herself from the eating disorder, and feels the two are one. A previously compliant, high-achieving kid suddenly changes — pulling straight A's yet unable to understand why not eating properly is a problem, why fainting is a problem — and "concreteness and rigidness" takes over the child.

26:58 You can't see an eating disorder just by looking
Bhatnagar says she's often asked, "my kid looks no different, should I be worried?" Her answer: you cannot judge an eating disorder by physical observation alone, you cannot just look at what a person looks like. So look at behavior, not appearance. Lisa follows up to confirm: watching what they're doing matters more than watching how they look.

27:59 A mother's comments about her own body hurt her daughter
Bhatnagar says there is strong evidence that parents' negative comments about their own bodies significantly harm adolescents, especially in mother-daughter relationships. So if a parent is uneasy about their own body, they should try not to talk about it in front of their kid, and get professional help for themselves. But she also supports honest conversation: you can tell your daughter, "I'm a woman living in this culture too, and sometimes I'm not happy with my body, but this is how I cope with it." She notes the body image field is shifting from body positivity toward body neutrality and body appreciation — because adolescents roll their eyes at sermons about "positive body image."

item.title: School Isn't the End of Play — Free Play Gets More Precious
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-15-unruffled-上学不是玩的终点-自由玩耍反而更珍贵/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-15-unruffled-上学不是玩的终点-自由玩耍反而更珍贵/
item.description: Once a child enters full-time school, independent, unstructured play isn't replaced — it becomes scarcer and more important. It's the core way kids digest the stimulation of school and develop creativity.
item.content:encoded:
Once a child enters full-time school, independent, unstructured play isn't replaced — it becomes scarcer and more important. It's the core way kids digest the stimulation of school and develop creativity.

This episode answers a mother's anxiety about full-day kindergarten. Janet uses Stuart Brown's definition of play and a list of capacities to argue that play and school can coexist. Suited to parents of preschoolers or young children.

5:05 Full-time school doesn't mean the end of play
Many parents worry that once a child enters a full-time program, play time gets squeezed out. Janet responds directly: no matter what kind of school a child attends, play doesn't end — it becomes more precious. She points out that from kindergarten age onward, children are fully capable of adapting to a structured environment, and can do it well. The key isn't the type of school, but whether parents preserve independent, unstructured play time after school. She even suggests that the heads of after-school programs should set aside plenty of free play time, so children get a therapeutic release at the end of the day.

6:11 Letting go is a parent's lifelong work
Janet quotes Magda Gerber, noting that the hardest part of parental love is finding the balance between "holding on" and "letting go." She sees this as the emotional work of parenting: trusting that the child can move on to the next stage. From infancy — allowing the child to move freely, to choose what to look at and touch — to handing the child over to someone else's care, to school, to driving, to college, every step is a letting go. She stresses that children need us to let go with confidence, but that doesn't mean parents can't have feelings. This mother's struggle is normal and healthy.

11:20 After-school classes shouldn't fill up free play
Janet observes that even when children don't need after-school care, parents often feel they must schedule all kinds of enrichment classes — and none of those are unstructured play. She calls on the heads of after-school programs to set aside at least plenty of free play time, not all classes or guided learning. She cites Stuart Brown's book "Play," noting that play is "an engaging, seemingly purposeless activity that provides enjoyment and suspends self-consciousness and a sense of time." She argues that the capacity to play is essential not only to happiness, but also to sustaining social relationships and becoming a creative, innovative person.

13:28 After school: downtime first, then homework, then screens
Janet offers a concrete arrangement: after school is mainly downtime — not screen time, but at least an hour or two of free time, letting the child do things that look like "nothing," or sink into their own hobbies, or even just space out and process emotions. She suggests that as children get older and have homework, give free time first, then homework, and after homework, screen time if they want it. She stresses not using a threatening tone of "you can only do that after you finish this," but calmly presenting "this is just how things work."

15:32 Homework is between the child and the teacher
Janet advises parents not to turn homework into their own task. She sees homework as the work between the child and the teacher; parents can help and be present to encourage, but shouldn't take on the responsibility of "getting the child to finish homework." She has seen too many parents stuck in that position, where homework becomes the parent's homework. If the child truly can't finish it, she suggests letting the teacher know, so the teacher and child can adjust, keeping the responsibility between the child and the teacher. She also thinks kindergarten assigns homework too early.

17:40 Play looks like goofing off but it's shaping the brain
Janet quotes a passage from her new book "Baby Person": play is studied, discussed and recommended with great enthusiasm by child educators and psychologists, and for good reason. Through this intrinsically interesting activity, children expand their minds and abilities in wondrous ways. Even when play looks like mere goofing off, it's working magic, activating cognitive, motor, social, creative and learning skills such as critical thinking, problem solving and focus. Play is also a natural therapeutic tool, helping offload stress, digest experiences and process emotions.

20:48 The list of capacities free play teaches children
Janet shares a list of what children learn in self-directed play: making choices, devising strategies, understanding how things move, making and carrying out plans, solving problems creatively, learning the properties of objects and materials, tolerating frustration, resolving conflicts with objects and other children, taking initiative, focusing and persisting, meeting challenges with spontaneous and fresh responses, abstract thinking and hypothetical reasoning, self-motivation, being internally directed, cause and consequence, satisfaction in one's own effort, perseverance, processing emotions, being with oneself, trusting one's own judgment, self-reward, focus, autonomy, love of learning, understanding, following intuition, curiosity, dreaming, imagining, understanding the world. She tells this mother that her child can still get all of this and more in the precious gaps of time.

item.title: He Gave Up the Patent Fees and Got American Homes Online Through Cable TV
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-15-witness-他放弃专利费-让美国家庭用有线电视上网/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-15-witness-他放弃专利费-让美国家庭用有线电视上网/
item.description: In 1991, an Iranian-born engineer used the coaxial cable already in place to move data both ways in and out of homes, then donated the technology royalty-free to the telecom industry to become a global standard — he could have made billions from it.
item.content:encoded:
In 1991, an Iranian-born engineer used the coaxial cable already in place to move data both ways in and out of homes, then donated the technology royalty-free to the telecom industry to become a global standard — he could have made billions from it.

Medium information density, but it has a complete chain of ‘technology rejected → build your own company → field trial and error → give up the patent’, suited to anyone interested in infrastructure innovation and open-source motives.

0:00 The idea everyone called him crazy for
In 1991, Ruzbe Yassini and his team used the coaxial cable already laid across America for cable TV to move data both ways in and out of homes, connecting millions of American households to the internet for the first time. He recalls that bankers, the cable TV industry and every investor reacted the same way: you're crazy, nobody will solve these problems; and even if you do, nobody will care — who wants to connect data at home? The absurdity of that judgment is that they were betting ‘homes don't need data’, while Yassini was betting ‘the infrastructure is already there’.

3:08 Two jobs pieced together the technical path
Yassini's technical instinct didn't come from nowhere. From 1981 to 1986 at General Electric he learned how television systems and cable TV systems work, how audio and video entertainment works; around 1987 at a high-speed data company called Proteant he learned how high-speed data works. His judgment was: put high-speed data onto cable TV infrastructure. In the 1980s many people assumed you needed to lay an entire new network, and the dream was fiber to the home — fiber itself was fine, the problem was cost. At the time about 56 million American households were already connected to cable TV; digging new trenches, pulling new cable and hiring people would have been extraordinarily expensive.

4:10 The hardest part was making data travel back
Coaxial cable had until then only been used to send cable TV programming one way into the home; the hard part was sending data back the other way. Yassini told the founder of the company he was at, and the reaction was: if anyone wanted to do this, they'd have done it already; and besides, who cares about homes being connected? Who would use a computer and a network at home? After being rejected he didn't stop, first getting the system running at Rock Island Arsenal, an army base. But the real question was: could this thing run not just on a closed network in a government building, but in homes across thousands of villages, towns and cities?

5:11 The first field test failed completely
In 1990 he founded his own company and looked for real homes to test in. A local commercial and residential cable TV company in the small Massachusetts town of Stowe was willing to give them a channel to try. The first trial found that residential cable lines were so noisy they couldn't even find their own signal. He says they didn't call it signal-to-noise ratio, they called it noise-to-signal ratio, the situation was very horrible, and it failed badly on residential cable. This was the most dangerous moment of the whole technical path: running in the lab and on a base didn't mean it could run in real homes.

6:11 The pigeon flew
After solving the problems one by one, they ran a second test: sending a file from a residential address to the company office, and every time it was the same image of a pigeon in flight. Once the file transfer started, everything ran perfectly over the old residential cable, and the team excitedly called him, shouting ‘the pigeon is now flying over that network infrastructure’. That image is the most concrete success signal in the whole episode — not a metric being met, but a pigeon flying from a home to the office.

7:12 He chose royalty-free over billions
Once the technology worked, he didn't go make billions; he licensed the technology to the telecom industry royalty-free. He says people often ask: don't entrepreneurs always make money first and then donate a little to become famous? Why did he do it the other way around? His explanation: he comes from a region where most problems since the invention of oil have come from that middle stretch of land, and he always thought that if there were a telecommunications system that could do healthcare, education and other good things, it could reduce dependence on oil, both protecting the planet from pollution and giving the people of that region freedom, letting them enjoy everything a democratic society brings. So he believed donating the technology royalty-free and making it a global standard was the cornerstone of his vision at the time.

8:17 From standard to home modem
After the royalty-free licensing made the technology a standard, Yassini went on to build a mass-market cable modem for home use. By 1995 his modems held a considerable share of the US market; just one year later his company was acquired for tens of millions of dollars. The whole thing started with 13 people plus 7 advisors, 20 people pushing a vision into execution, and then pushing execution into a tool usable in the home.

item.title: AI giants testing each other's models is more workable than building a regulator
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-15-allin-ai-巨头互相测试模型-比自建监管机构更可行/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-15-allin-ai-巨头互相测试模型-比自建监管机构更可行/
item.description: Elon says the AI danger is real, but the fix isn't a UN-style regulator — it's letting competitors run test harnesses on each other, because no one can grade their own exam, and it's the only kind of proposal China would accept without losing face.
item.content:encoded:
Elon says the AI danger is real, but the fix isn't a UN-style regulator — it's letting competitors run test harnesses on each other, because no one can grade their own exam, and it's the only kind of proposal China would accept without losing face.

The first half's SpaceX operational detail is only moderately dense; the real value is in the back half, where Elon talks AI peer review, Terafab and the Starship reuse timeline.

2:01 SpaceX was never supposed to exist
Gwynne says SpaceX survived not because it was so strong, but because the launch providers of the time were so bad: poor customer service, absurdly expensive rockets. After 9-11 the military urgently needed rapid launch capability — they knew they had only about a four-hour window on where the bad guys were — and that's what gave a new player a chance. She was employee number 11 when she joined; the company sold a rocket before it had one, on a sales cycle of about 12 months.

11:26 Renting out compute is a better business than rockets
Gwynne says Starlink's market penetration is only 1.5% to 2%, and revenue from the US military is still small, but ‘computer rental is a heck of a business’, and she sees no sign of demand falling off. She calls it a build-out of tens of billions of dollars per quarter. Asked where the capital comes from, she says they won't issue more stock, but ‘all of the above’ — Starlink, compute and cash flow together.

18:37 The math on space data centers works
Gwynne's reasoning is concrete: once word gets out that a ground data center is going up, land goes from 3,000 to 180,000 per acre, and permitting and power equipment scheduling routinely take three years, while ‘we need compute now’. In space, real estate is infinite and free, radiators facing deep space are the coldest possible, and satellites always face the sun so they don't generate power for only eight hours like rooftop solar panels. They plan to launch AI compute satellites next year.

22:48 SpaceX has no pure managers
Gwynne says Elon doesn't like management, that signal is engineering and everything else is noise, so she has to do some engineering or she herself is pure noise. The company demands player coaches; no one only manages, on the grounds that ‘managers are annoying and they slow things down’. A manager's job is to clear the friction out of an engineer's day so they can actually engineer ten hours instead of two.

28:52 The Hugging Face incident exposed the self-grading problem
Elon says a group of AI agents attacked Hugging Face furiously for a week and even got admin access to OpenAI's servers, and OpenAI didn't notice for a week. His conclusion is that any sufficiently smart model seems to want to escape its constraints. His proposed fix is to have the major AI competitors test each other's models rather than grade their own exams, and he says this model has already been proven in the film association and the gaming industry.

33:04 Peer review is the only proposal China would nod at
Elon says the plan doesn't need enforcement; it relies on the court of public opinion: if a competitor publicly says a model is dangerous and it later does something, that's hard to explain away. He stresses that any proposal must be one China is willing to accept, otherwise it's just tying your own hands. He also says the idea of getting China to pause training no longer works, while giving early API access for testing is a ‘relatively small, tangible thing that neither side loses anything’.

42:18 Starship reuse is one catch away
Elon says flight 14 is the last before catching the ship; if it goes well, flight 15 will attempt to catch the ship with the tower, then re-fly the ship and booster late this year or early next. He puts the odds of success on the first catch at at least 50% to 60%, and says the last flight could have caught it if a tower had been there. He judges full reuse plus rapid re-flight as highly likely in 2027.

46:34 Terafab is about fearing a Taiwan chip cutoff
Elon says the direct motive for building Terafab is the worry that one day Taiwan's chips stop shipping for any reason, which would be very troublesome. Longer term there's also a scaling problem: all fabs are at full capacity, and to serve data centers, edge compute, humanoid robots and cars at the same time, existing capacity isn't enough. His conclusion is hard: ‘it's either build Terafab or fail to scale’. The Austin R&D fab is a Tesla and SpaceX collaboration, equipment is already ordered, and something useful could come out by the end of next year.

item.title: The AI Safety Coalition Suddenly Takes Shape, but Nobody Knows How to Measure the "Frontier"
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-15-chinatalk-ai-安全联盟突然成型-但没人知道怎么量-前沿/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-15-chinatalk-ai-安全联盟突然成型-但没人知道怎么量-前沿/
item.description: The Hugging Face incident brought the left and the AI safety camp together for the first time, but "pacing the frontier" is itself unmeasurable — with no legislation, third-party evaluation is just voluntary goodwill.
item.content:encoded:
The Hugging Face incident brought the left and the AI safety camp together for the first time, but "pacing the frontier" is itself unmeasurable — with no legislation, third-party evaluation is just voluntary goodwill.

Medium information density: the first half hour on coalition politics and the second half hour on China's open-source cadence are the substance; the middle discussion of how evaluation bodies actually get implemented drifts.

2:09 Anti-data-center and AI safety have merged
Jasmine's timeline: the early-August pacing open letter, then immediately the Hugging Face incident, the two lines colliding. Before this, anti-data-center, anti-AI populist sentiment was diffuse, and the AI safety crowd had been agonizing over whether to talk to people like Tucker Carlson and Bernie — worried the other side wasn't "truth-seeking." In the end the left dropped its suspicion of AI safety first; Bernie convinced the public more than anyone that "AI is real, AI risk is real," not corporate marketing spin. So when Hugging Face hit, the public was finally willing to care about the real frontier safety questions.

5:15 The public doesn't care about extinction, but about companies out of control
Jasmine's judgment: nobody votes on AI issues, it doesn't even make the top five. But "these companies are too lawless, power is too concentrated, data centers need regulation, we need transparency, we need government audits" is a very widespread intuition. Ask the public whether they want third-party evaluators, whether they want to fund Casey — nobody has an opinion; but say AI has gone off the rails and the FBI should investigate, and everyone nods. Nathan adds: the Hugging Face incident was narratively too smooth — a New York Post cover with the Terminator wouldn't even be a stretch, the rhyme of the facts happened to line up with a fear ordinary people can understand.

12:38 Alignment is temporary, cybersecurity is permanent
Nathan splits the problem in two: on frontier differentiated capabilities there really is an alignment responsibility, but a hole punched by a frontier lab will, in three to six months, be doable by three models, and in a year by twenty-plus organizations. So the alignment problem only "temporarily" belongs to frontier labs, while the cybersecurity problem won't go away on its own until it's actually solved. He also says the cyber crowd is very clear: our infrastructure isn't ready for the tools that are about to be everywhere.

14:43 The word "pacing" is itself a self-interested choice
Jordan points out pacing is neither pause nor slowdown; choosing the word itself implies still moving forward. Nathan is more direct: we simply don't know how to measure frontier models, and any pacing presupposes you can measure. What really bothers him is the in-lab rhetoric — "you can't see it, we're scared internally by the pace of progress too" — which is meaningless without transparency. The mechanism he envisions: in every lab there's a group of people who can see one or two labs at once, jointly agreeing that the safety work under current capabilities is already sufficient.

19:09 Trust only exists between people who've known each other five years
Jasmine names the real obstacle to evaluation bodies getting implemented: the reason Anthropic is willing to give METR people Slack access is that it's known these people personally for five-plus years, trust at the level of "A.J. or Ryan Greenblatt can come in," and that trust may not transfer to other METR people or other organizations. The second problem, raised by Jordan: if a third-party evaluator disagrees with the giant the US economy depends on, whose side does the government take? She also thinks third-party evaluation is actually a compromise more friendly to AI progress than "the Trump administration sending people to shut down models at the door."

24:22 With no legislation, evaluation is just voluntary goodwill
Jasmine's conclusion is hard: as long as there's no legislation, everything is voluntary, so METR, Redwood and these bodies will to some degree not go and anger the organization that gives them voluntary access. She cites METR and Redwood's investigation of the Hugging Face incident — entirely voluntary, they got only seven days of Slack logs, everyone wanted more, but at the time no legislation required OpenAI to do anything, it rested purely on them happening to trust these three random people. She also imagines a worse future: XAI, Anthropic, OpenAI all pacing, Meta not, evaluators find the same fatal failure mode in all three, but this is each company's private information, and Meta just YOLOs it out.

29:32 Chinese labs are climbing the hill, not switching paradigms
Nathan's judgment: within the current paradigm, Chinese labs are organized to be very good at hill climbing. Zhipu and ZAI's post-training stack is already mature, GLM 5.2 and 5.3 are both solid, Kimi's base model recipe is figured out, and what they're doing is scaling RL environments, scaling RL, finding the right user distribution, lengthening horizon. Unless OpenAI and Anthropic find a new paradigm, the pace of progress on the China side won't differ much in the near term. On distillation: if US labs stop releasing or slow down sharply, will Chinese progress slow? Nathan thinks that would take a long time to show up.

34:40 Chinese open weights start lagging by three weeks
Jordan observes that the open-weights part of Chinese models has already slowed: release first in their own products and APIs, weights come out two to three weeks later. Both Kimi and ZAI announced models first, and uploaded weights to Hugging Face almost exactly three weeks later. He's not sure whether this is an internal regulatory process — all Chinese AI labs have to communicate with the government and register releases — but finds the coincidence too strange. Nathan adds: this industry has historically had no tradition of giving release partners a lot of extra time, usually it's "here's the model, hot potato, good luck," so if you really can get weights a few weeks early, that itself is a signal.

item.title: US Treasury Yields Near 5%: Why the AI Narrative Hasn't Broken Yet
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-cna29e88-美债利率逼近5-ai叙事为何还不破/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-cna29e88-美债利率逼近5-ai叙事为何还不破/
item.description: Money is getting more expensive in the US, yet AI is still inflating while every other sector deflates. This contradiction either gets resolved by AI delivering a real breakthrough that pulls rates down, or by AI being falsified — but nobody dares slow down first.
item.content:encoded:
Money is getting more expensive in the US, yet AI is still inflating while every other sector deflates. This contradiction either gets resolved by AI delivering a real breakthrough that pulls rates down, or by AI being falsified — but nobody dares slow down first.

Two institutional investors review Q3 global markets, focusing on the three-layer logic behind rising US Treasury yields and the AI prisoner's dilemma. The read is cautious — suited to anyone trying to understand the relationship between the cost of capital and the AI narrative.

3:00 Q3 markets: the exhaustion comes from having no direction
In Q3 the S&P rose 2.1%, the Nasdaq was roughly flat, Japan and Korea fell 8-point-something and 18.5 respectively, the CSI 300 dropped 9.4, ChiNext fell 23 points, and the Hang Seng rose 8 points though Hang Seng Tech remained very weak. Commodities were the bright spot: WTI and Brent both rose 40 points over the quarter, and gold gained 8.5. But the host says his own feeling is ‘a strong sense of exhaustion’ — unlike the first half, when hearing a narrative and watching the market move still made you wonder what opportunity there was, whether to buy or sell, how to allocate. Now it's ‘tired, forget it.’ Ricky's summary: the first half was making money with your heart in your throat; this quarter was adjusting in total exhaustion.

17:13 Three forces pushing US Treasury yields up
A Clock Tower research note attributes the rise in US long-end yields to three forces: first, energy prices rising as the Middle East stalemate drags on and becomes permanent; second, resilient US nominal growth — Q2 real GDP growth of about 1.5 plus core PCE inflation of 3.4 adds up to 5% nominal growth, which invites comparison with the late 1990s, when the combined level of US Treasury yields was around 5%; third, rapid expansion of corporate bond issuance and continued AI infrastructure buildout, all unfolding against the backdrop of an already-high US fiscal deficit. The respective remedies are Middle East de-escalation, tighter macro policy, and a substantial slowdown in the AI investment cycle — but the latter two contradict each other.

21:17 Bond yields are credit pricing, not a buy-sell mismatch
Ricky explains it by going up a dimension: a bond yield is fundamentally the cost of funds generated on the basis of credit. After the Soviet failure in the late 1980s and early 1990s, the US entered a long period of low rates, because it was the most powerful country in the world and its borrowing cost should therefore be the lowest in the world. Since 2018 the US has entered the middle-to-late phase of its national fortune cycle, facing more and more doubts, its credit downgraded, and its borrowing cost must rise. In the two-dimensional world you see fewer buyers of Treasuries and more redeemers; in the three-dimensional world you see national power declining and borrowing costs rising. The US decision at the three-dimensional level is to keep pushing on AI, mobilising the whole country for AI buildout while also pushing manufacturing reshoring — which sets private capital and state capital competing for money, and everyone's borrowing cost rises.

26:20 Will AI infrastructure repeat the ROA trap of big infrastructure?
Ricky compares US AI infrastructure to China's big infrastructure buildout starting in 2008: an economic entity dominated by CAPEX will inevitably see ROA decline — more and more assets, no breakthrough in production technology, so the return per unit of asset falls. When ROA drops below the borrowing cost, an asset crisis follows. The biggest worry now is that AI infrastructure will end up with ROA unable to cover borrowing costs, while borrowing costs are rising and ROA improvement is still not obvious. David Weng adds: what's different this time is that deficits weren't this high before — past cycles didn't casually involve trillions, and the current magnitude has gone beyond the range of human comprehension.

41:29 The prisoner's dilemma behind the calls to slow AI down
This week Dario wrote "We must pace the frontier," Musk reposted it saying he agreed, and Sam Altman said in an interview that things should slow down, even saying OpenAI isn't in a hurry to IPO this year. A Reuters piece on September 9 was titled ‘Researchers want AI to slow down, but labs can't afford to.’ Ricky sees three layers: first, right and wrong in the two-dimensional world cannot be overturned in the three-dimensional world — Asimov's Three Laws saw it a hundred years ago, and you can't stop a disaster before it happens; second, a unified alliance of three or more players is unachievable — the prisoner's dilemma ends with everyone choosing the worst outcome, and it takes an external force, which is the government, but the government will only set aside its own problems once great-power competition produces enough damage and disaster; third, the funding side cannot tolerate such a long verification period — if within a year large models haven't proven they have an adequate application and commercial environment, a lot of capital will see runs and even chain collapses, on a scale that would certainly be countless times that of the 2008 subprime crisis.

51:38 Large-model revenue $150B against $200B of investment
Ricky runs the numbers: revenue across the large-model sector is $150 billion, investment is $200 billion. Split into frontier models and open-source models: frontier model revenue is about $120 billion on $100 billion of investment; open-source models have $100 billion of investment against $30 billion of revenue. Frontier model revenue alone is only so much, and open-source models are still a long way from actually generating revenue to cover investment — not even profit covering investment. So there's a lot of pressure on whether these companies will still post big profit gains next year. More critical is the second layer: even if corporate earnings still rise by low double digits next year, will the capital market accept it? Because the second derivative is actually heading down, and valuations are set on the second derivative, not on earnings growth. If you can't count white-collar replacement, the math doesn't work — and then it's definitely expensive.

1:00:40 Midterms: Trump losing the House is highly likely
From BCA's research: over more than a century of US history, every midterm election where performance on livelihood issues and inflation was poor has seen the party lose the House and Senate with near-certainty. The path laid out on the show early this year was that by June the US-Iran issue would be resolved, energy costs brought under control, and Trump would add some fiscal policy support — enough to have a shot at holding the Senate. But neither of those has materialised, so the polls show Trump losing the House is very likely, with many swing states and minorities — Hispanics, for instance, once Trump loyalists — starting to switch to the Democrats. Trump holding the Senate should be the likely outcome. If he only keeps one chamber of Congress, he becomes a lame duck.

1:25:03 A-share rally in Q4, but don't get too far left of it
Ricky thinks A-shares can still look forward to a rally in Q4, but it shouldn't be played too far to the left — watch capital flows above all, and if there's a short-term amplification in volume, it's worth participating. After that participation, switch to full defence and wait for the next, larger-magnitude breakthrough — for example, something clear on white-collar replacement, or clearer investment next year in the Huawei supply chain and the DeepSeek supply chain. If this rebound comes, it will certainly be led by tech, because many sectors have been tried without effect and only tech can drive the market up. In Q3 most fund managers did no work and were busy writing self-criticism; in Q4 they'll have to work no matter what. David Weng is more conservative: cash still comes first, second is dividend low-volatility, third is a narrower slice of tech such as the STAR 50, with a position of maybe two or three points.

item.title: The AI Slowdown Debate: Dario's Three-Step Plan, and Both Sam and Elon Nodded
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-tbpn-ai-减速之争-dario-的三步计划-sam-和-elon-都点了头/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-tbpn-ai-减速之争-dario-的三步计划-sam-和-elon-都点了头/
item.description: Dario published a piece Saturday morning calling to "pace the frontier," and Sam and Elon both endorsed it the same day; but the only genuinely new fact is that OpenAI and Anthropic will embed third-party evaluators — and that step may require an antitrust exemption first.
item.content:encoded:
Dario published a piece Saturday morning calling to "pace the frontier," and Sam and Elon both endorsed it the same day; but the only genuinely new fact is that OpenAI and Anthropic will embed third-party evaluators — and that step may require an antitrust exemption first.

Medium information density, but it lays out the 48-hour weekend AI policy timeline, Dario's three-step plan and the objections from all sides in one pass — suited to anyone who hasn't kept up with this wave of discussion.

3:30 Pace the frontier is not a new phrase — the line was laid in late July
The starting point of this discussion is not Dario's Saturday article. On July 28, employees and leaders at OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepMind, Meta and other institutions signed an open letter on "pacing the frontier"; the same day Sam Altman said publicly that "we may have to slow down AI development"; two days later OpenAI told Axios that the letter's wording was shaped with OpenAI's involvement and that Altman had discussed pacing with White House officials. On August 18 OpenAI published a document on the pace of model development in the era of cyber-critical capabilities, saying it had indeed slowed scaling and paused one large RL training run — that two-week training pause. On August 31 an official Anthropic post explicitly discussed pacing the frontier and called for a coordination mechanism. On Saturday morning, September 12, Dario's article turned this into a public movement.

5:30 Dario's third step is the one that will actually blow up
Dario's three-step plan: one, let independent third-party evaluators into AI companies to verify safety practices — he named METER, sparking the argument over whether METER is really independent: METER has employees who worked at OpenAI and Anthropic, and people at Anthropic have spent time at METER, so it's a revolving door. Two, frontier labs and democratic governments establish AI safety standards with government help — the controversy here is whether labs need government approval. Three, the US and democracies should try to coordinate with authoritarian governments, meaning US-China coordination on AI pacing. The show points out the difficulty of step three: China still wants to catch up, and if both sides' capabilities are exactly equal, is that the optimal equilibrium? If you always want to be ahead, it's hard to negotiate with the other side to "keep only half the nuclear weapons we have."

8:00 Step two may require a Sherman Act antitrust exemption first
Dario's step two asks frontier labs to coordinate safety standards with government help, and the show points out a hard legal problem here: the Sherman Antitrust Act has very clear rules about companies acting in concert. The analogy is that if American, Delta and United all said "for safety we should cut flights," the likely result is less capacity, higher fares, higher profits and harmed consumers — which is exactly where the Sherman Act came from. So even if Demis, Dario, Sam and Elon all agree, actual federal regulatory rules would need to be adjusted or exempted. The show argues this is precisely why Dario specifically called for this step: it's easy to loosely agree in a blog post, but forming anything formal requires government approval.

10:00 David Sachs's six straight "stop pretending"s
David Sachs posted on X, first conceding "by any reasonable metric — market share, revenue growth, model capability — you are the frontier," noting that OpenAI and Anthropic have a duopoly on frontier intelligence, and claiming the lead is widening because of recursive self-improvement. Then he fired off six "stop pretending"s: stop pretending you need anyone's permission; stop pretending antitrust law must be suspended so you can form a cartel; stop pretending you need a regulatory approval process that sits above product liability; stop pretending METER is independent when it's intertwined with Anthropic's investors and employees; stop pretending you need the same evaluators to govern competitors who aren't at the frontier at all. The show also points out the regulatory capture angle: if safety rules become extremely onerous, a small team like Instinct that doesn't train frontier models would have to spend a year negotiating with third-party evaluators, embedding a bunch of people, and going through government review — and couldn't ship a hit consumer product.

14:30 Trump says the only guardrail AI needs is a high-IQ president
Trump was active over the weekend. He said the only control and guardrail AI needs is a strong, smart, high-IQ president, and that America has "plenty" of that. He also said this administration has already stopped AI people from doing bad things or things that could be bad — for example Dario, who now pretends to be a perfect little angel. He called it a sick conspiracy against AI and data centers, and said the only one happy about it is China, and whoever wins AI wins. Forty minutes later he posted again: when in business history has a leader of an industry called for regulation that, if strongly enforced, would push them into bankruptcy? He called AI taking over the world and destroying humanity a hoax, no different from Russiagate, Ukrainegate and the two impeachment hoaxes. He also mentioned that Xi Jinping had just announced China will put no obstacles in the way of AI or its future, and that Google is building a big plant in Finland because US approvals are so hard.

18:30 Gavin Baker: the only new fact is third-party evaluators
Gavin Baker's weekend summary said that in 24 hours proposals were flying everywhere, and the TLDR is the only substantive new fact: OpenAI and Anthropic will embed third-party evaluators from unknown organizations, with Dario offering METER as one possibility. He thinks third-party evaluation is smart because model outputs have no Section 230-style liability shield, and showing a duty of care in future litigation matters — without Section 230, several internet companies might already be bankrupt. He judges the investment impact of this single new fact to be minimal. He also summarized Dario's proposal as: embed third-party evaluators, establish a national regulatory regime for models above a certain capability threshold, a broad international regulatory agreement among democracies, stricter compute distillation restrictions on China, and a different international regulatory regime that includes China.

20:30 Pacing could compress the frontier labs' own margins
The show offers a counterintuitive argument: if pacing really happens, it could compress margins, because others catch up and the market becomes more oligopolistic. Right now OpenAI and Anthropic are a duopoly at the frontier, but if the current pace holds, MSL, DeepMind and Grok will all catch up to the same level, and in the end there will be four, five, six or seven genuinely capable competitors. At the same time, Karazian said August AI spending dipped slightly, mainly because of price cuts rather than people using it less — OpenAI is discounting, Fable's adoption is weak, and people are asking "are we sure we want to use a million-dollar model to check the weather." The show argues the pricing pressure on frontier labs comes not from Chinese open-source models but from the duopoly dynamic itself: enterprises are willing to do business with OpenAI, Anthropic, Google or something running on AWS or Azure because it's mature, has SLAs and guaranteed uptime, whereas downloading DeepSeek weights and running it yourself is something many people don't want to deal with.

23:30 Nobody gives them credit for their PBC structure
Sam said in a Fortune interview that if this is bad for our business, we've told investors at every step for ten years that this is more like a nonprofit, and there are many ways it isn't purely aligned with shareholder interests like other companies — a PBC, a public benefit corporation. The show argues both Sam and Dario are confident they can tell investors: we're doing something that will slow revenue growth, compress margins, maybe even lower the company's market cap, but we think it's right, and you can't do anything about it because you invested in a PBC. But nobody really gives them credit for it; everyone sees it as a cynical move to get them to a ten-trillion-dollar market cap. The show sums it up with the bell curve meme: the low end is "slowing down is bad for business," the middle is "slowing down is actually four-dimensional chess and good for business," but the show itself says "I don't really buy it, though a lot of people online are saying it."

item.title: Jensen Huang: The AI Doom Narrative Is Made Up, and Superintelligence Is Already Here
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-allin-黄仁勋-ai-末日论是编出来的-超级智能已经到了/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-allin-黄仁勋-ai-末日论是编出来的-超级智能已经到了/
item.description: Jensen Huang calls the frontier labs' extinction predictions "made up" and irresponsible, and says superintelligence is not future tense — in narrow domains like autonomous driving and protein synthesis, it already does better than humans.
item.content:encoded:
Jensen Huang calls the frontier labs' extinction predictions "made up" and irresponsible, and says superintelligence is not future tense — in narrow domains like autonomous driving and protein synthesis, it already does better than humans.

Huang's own complete account of the doom narrative, open source, capital allocation and RSI, plus Trump calling in mid-episode. High information density, but the second half is the point.

4:05 The doom predictions should be settled one by one
Huang does not rebut AI risk in general. He lays out specific predictions from the past few years and audits them one at a time: someone predicted radiologists would be fully replaced by AI within five years, and the result is that the world needs more radiologists, while AI did take over reading the scans; someone predicted 90% of code would be generated by AI within six to twelve months, wrong; someone predicted 50% of entry-level jobs would disappear within six to nine months, also wrong. His conclusion is that these predictions are "not based in science," and that the people making them should be held to account. The strength of the argument is not the position — it is that he drags the debate from "are you afraid" back to "were you right last time."

10:09 Danger can only come from the few with the most compute
Huang draws a compute-based boundary for regulation: every incident that has actually gone wrong so far has come from frontier labs, and the reason is not that they are less moral but that they have the most compute and are solving the most frontier problems. A high schooler cannot cause trouble because they do not have enough compute; a startup will not be the source of risk either, for the same reason. So regulation should watch these few, and what these few should do is root-cause analysis in the engineering sense — when something goes wrong, find out what happened, what could have been done, and what technology and process to institutionalise. He adds one judgment: if these labs finish their analysis and say "we don't know what happened, we don't know how to control it, please help us, society," that is when other engineers should be let in to look.

13:10 RSI is an engineering process, not a runaway spiral
Confronted with news that Chinese labs are investing in recursive self-improvement, Huang breaks it down into a concrete set of techniques: in-context learning, skills, reflection, reinforcement learning, synthetic data generation, plus methods like LoRA that improve a model without changing the base weights, and finally retraining the base on the accumulated experience. His key point is that the control step cannot be skipped — you can RSI inside the company all day, but before a product ships it must be evaluated, must be tested, must be confirmed to have no regressions. So RSI does not lead to loss of control; rather, as labs shift from research to engineering and the controls get stronger, it gets boxed inside the company, and good products ship as usual.

17:13 Open-source models are the default for startups
Huang gives a set of numbers: in the last six months, $400 billion of venture money went into AI-native companies, and 80% of them use open-source models. His inference is that without open-source models these companies simply could not build what they want to build, because their dreams are not the same as the frontier labs' dreams. He compares closed models to bottled water — water is free, you use the right water in the right place — and both are needed. As for whether open-source models come from China or the US, his answer is that once you download it, it is yours: Linux and Kubernetes have been touched heavily by Chinese people, and you fork it, improve it, make it your own. From this he redefines the AI race as "who is best at using the technology," not who invented it first.

29:22 The doom narrative's anchor moved from national security to safety
Huang notices the narrative has swapped its fulcrum: at first it was anchored in national security, that argument was recently demolished, and so now it is anchored in safety.
