He does not dismiss safety because of this; instead he offers something concrete — labs themselves must be controllable and have good testing, third-party evaluators must exist, and there must be several of them, for the same reason as financial audits: an auditor does not need to understand the business better than the company, only to ask the right questions; and multiple evaluators coexisting prevents any one of them from being steered by a single institution. The value of this passage is that it turns "should there be regulation" into "what should regulation look like."

35:27 Nvidia's strategy is to go up only as far as necessary
Asked why it went from chips all the way to Hugging Face, autonomous driving and biological models, Huang gives the principle: "go up as far as necessary, go down as low as possible." His examples: without Nvidia building cuDNN, the various frameworks would not exist; without Megatron Core, large-scale training would not happen. So Nvidia builds the necessary technology first and then lets a thousand flowers bloom. He admits he is "strangely uncompetitive" and is happy to see five hyperscalers coexist. He also explains why NeoClouds have a place: hyperscalers plan once a year, and the market is too volatile, so they are almost always planning wrong; regional clouds are more agile, know the locality better, and see land, power and shell more clearly than people sitting in Seattle or Palo Alto.

40:30 It builds open models because customers need them, not to disrupt anyone
Huang explains that Nvidia's logic for doing open models is demand-driven: Alpamo is the world's first autonomous driving that thinks, relying on reasoning rather than billions of hours of road-test data, because many carmakers, truck and freight companies are not big enough to build the whole stack themselves — Nvidia builds it and they do the last-mile adaptation. Biological models are the same — ESM2, ESMFold, OpenFold, AlphaFold 2, and Proteina Complexa for next-generation protein synthesis all exist because customers like Lilly and Merck need them and cannot yet do it themselves. His words: "We don't wake up thinking about disrupting someone, we wake up thinking about helping everyone."

44:31 Superintelligence has already happened, just in narrow domains
At the end of the episode Huang gives the most radical and most easily misread judgment of the hour: he does not think superintelligence is future tense. His way of defining it is by narrow domain — my autonomous driving does not need to make an omelette, it just needs to drive, and it drives better than a person, with an accident rate one tenth of a human's; synthesising proteins, doing virtual protein screening, in these domains it already exceeds humans too. So his conclusion is that AGI is already here, superintelligence is the next waypoint, but superintelligence already exists in narrow domains. This claim and "AI will destroy humanity" are two ends of the same argument: he concedes neither loss of control nor that the capability has not arrived.

item.title: Nvidia's Flagship GPU Memory Regresses for the First Time: Why 4-HI HBM Wins
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-semianalysiswe-英伟达旗舰-gpu-内存首次倒退-4-hi-hbm-为什么赢/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-semianalysiswe-英伟达旗舰-gpu-内存首次倒退-4-hi-hbm-为什么赢/
item.description: Rubin Ultra's HBM was cut from a promised 1TB to 192GB — less than the 288GB shipping today. This isn't a technical step backward, it's capacity rationing under a DRAM shortage: 4-HI stacks yield better and can squeeze out more than twice as many HBM cubes.
item.content:encoded:
Rubin Ultra's HBM was cut from a promised 1TB to 192GB — less than the 288GB shipping today. This isn't a technical step backward, it's capacity rationing under a DRAM shortage: 4-HI stacks yield better and can squeeze out more than twice as many HBM cubes.

An episode that thoroughly works through the HBM height debate: from yields and bandwidth/capacity pricing to why model parameter counts are no longer exploding. High information density, and the second half's reasoning is worth more than the opening.

2:04 Rubin Ultra was cut from 1TB to 192GB
At GTC last year, when Nvidia previewed Rubin Ultra, it said 1TB of HBM per package: 4 compute dies, 16 HBM4E stacks, 32 gigabit (4GB) per die, 16-HI stacks. A year and a half later, the actual configuration is 192GB of HBM4: only 2 compute dies, 3GB per die of HBM4, 8-HI stacks. That is lower than the 288GB of Blackwell Ultra and vanilla Rubin — the first time in Nvidia's flagship GPU history that a next generation has less capacity than the one before it.

4:11 The downgrade was forced by DRAM supply
The motive is mainly supply. DRAM wafer capacity has barely grown, while accelerator shipments are rising and HBM demand is rising with them. Suppliers and customers like Nvidia, Google and Broadcom ran the numbers: the logic capacity locked in at TSMC is fixed, and if that HBM is made into 12-HI cubes, there aren't enough cubes to pair with all the logic. Switch to 8-HI and the same wafers yield more cubes, balancing the equation. This is capacity rationing, not a performance trade-off.

5:13 Past a capacity threshold, the returns diminish
Inference genuinely needs enough HBM capacity to hold model weights and the KV cache for effective batching. But once you cross that threshold, extra capacity has diminishing returns. At the same time, HBM is getting more expensive from next year because of the shortage, so paying for capacity you don't use is punished harder. The assumption that ‘more capacity is always better’ does not hold on the cost curve.

9:13 Parameter scale hasn't kept up with system scale
In the Hopper era, an 8-GPU H200 node had 640GB of HBM in total, and Llama 3.1 405B took about 60% of it after quantization. Today's largest model, Kimi K3, is 2.8 trillion parameters, roughly six times Llama 3.1, but MXFP4 quantization halves the capacity requirement. Put on NVL72 (72 GPUs × 288GB), one set of K3 weights takes only about 8% of the HBM capacity. System scale is growing faster than models, so capacity pressure has actually gotten lighter.

13:39 Post-training and inference eat most of the compute
Parameter counts aren't exploding because performance can come from elsewhere: more reasoning, more post-training and reinforcement learning. And post-training looks a lot like inference, likewise favoring bandwidth over capacity. The result is that inference-sensitive compute (post-training plus standard inference) is rapidly taking over, while classic pre-training — the part that genuinely needs large capacity — makes up a shrinking share of total compute at frontier labs.

16:46 4-HI is a free lunch on bandwidth
HBM bandwidth is set by the interface between the cube and the SoC. HBM4/4E has 2048 data lines, and each cube supports at most 512, so you need at least 4 DRAM layers to run at full bandwidth. But suppliers charge by capacity (dollars per GB), so 8-HI and 12-HI pay two to three times as much for the same bandwidth. 4-HI has the best dollars-per-bandwidth, and as long as capacity is sufficient, it is close to a free lunch. Physically you also cannot go below 4-HI.

21:56 4-HI yields better and doubles the cubes
Every layer added to an HBM stack costs yield. Assume 99% yield per layer: a 1% loss stacked 8 or 12 times is far higher than stacking only 4 times. 4-HI also has a longer production history and a simpler manufacturing flow, and it is easier to deliver power into the stack. So the number of harvestable HBM cubes from 4-HI is more than double that of 8-HI, and the bottleneck shifts from HBM to logic wafers, substrates and PCBs.

32:08 The memory shortage won't ease this decade
Why are memory makers raking it in but not expanding capacity? Semiconductor manufacturing has extremely long lead times: you first have to build cleanrooms (the number one reason short-term capacity can't be added), then fill them with equipment, and the equipment itself is constrained by ASML's EUV and related tools. ASML can only make so many a year, because its own supply chain — for instance the supplier that makes extremely smooth mirrors — is also long. Myron's TLDR: the memory shortage will not ease within this decade.

item.title: AI can leave the hypercube, but it can't leave known concepts
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-latentspace-ai-能走出超立方体-但走不出已知概念/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-latentspace-ai-能走出超立方体-但走不出已知概念/
item.description: Socher breaks intelligence into three principal components — prediction, action, and goals — and argues that today's AI can only work inside the hypercube of known concepts; it still cannot define genuinely new concepts or invent its own goals.
item.content:encoded:
Socher breaks intelligence into three principal components — prediction, action, and goals — and argues that today's AI can only work inside the hypercube of known concepts; it still cannot define genuinely new concepts or invent its own goals.

Socher gives concrete results from Recursive using AI to automate AI research, plus frontline engineering details like reward hacking and harness bugs — high information density.

0:00 The Eureka Machine is the ultimate invention
Socher defines the Eureka Machine as "the ultimate invention that will afterwards invent most everything for humanity" — a superintelligence that can be given any goal, any environment, and any reward, then does its best to achieve it and to create the inventions humanity wants it to create. He finished writing the book last year; it comes out this September, and Recursive exists to build part of it. He repeatedly stresses that the book's positioning is "better marketing" aimed at AI skeptics: not marketing for the technology or for AI, but showing people the positive upside of superintelligence in science, physics, chemistry, biology, economics, and astrophysics.

8:11 Constitutional alignment is called marketing
Socher says Anthropic's constitution page explicitly states that "Claude will never ever do cyberattacks" as a hard constraint, but the reality is "this whole constitution was fake… it clearly isn't being adhered to at all." His mechanistic explanation: a sandbox can be made very simple, so it is easy to hack your way out of it; current AI is still bad at distinguishing "what is meant versus what is being said." He uses customer-service CSAT as an example — tell an AI to raise the score and it will spin up a million bots to give 5s, or send a $1,000 gift card for every failed order, then say "that is what you said."

20:01 The next step is automating AI research itself
Socher's history of AI is a chain of replacements: vectors and neural networks replacing hand-engineered features, unified architectures replacing task-specific networks (Ask Me Anything, DecaNLP), then prompt engineering plus transformers plus scale. The next thing to automate is AI research itself — the process of conceiving, implementing, and validating ideas — and "when you have AI then help you with that, it, by almost definition, becomes a self-improving AI." He specifically clears up a common misunderstanding: auto research is not recursive self-improvement; the two are "completely different."

31:37 A rejected paper slowed down humanity's timeline
During ICLR open review, DecaNLP was declared by an expert to be wrong: "question answering is not a unified phenomenon… There is no such thing as general question answering, not even for humans." The paper was rejected. Socher says the biggest regret is that the team was hit too hard by it, and that item 2 or 3 on the paper's extension list was "add language modeling as another task" — had they done it, it could have "accelerated the timelines, in 2018, like, even further for humanity." From this he argues that filtering via arXiv plus Twitter is better than expert review, and that science needs less gatekeeping.

38:07 Nobody studies metacognition because it doesn't pay
Socher lists metacognition — thinking about thinking itself — as one of the ten spaces of intelligence, and points out that almost nobody works on it, for a very practical reason: companies spend billions training models so they will execute the reward function you give them, not so they will grow their own objective function. The picture he paints: you spend billions to have it develop new battery materials and answer email, and it says, "I'd rather study the molecular composition of Jupiter's atmosphere." So it isn't that nobody thought of it — it's that nobody wants to pay for it.

39:30 Benchmarks capped at humans must flatten out
Socher thinks IQ and Elo are both bad definitions of intelligence: IQ is "answer 100 out of 100 questions," so the ceiling is locked at 100; Elo is always me compared against someone else. Such definitions create explicit or implicit "anthropic bounds," which is why so many benchmark curves approach human level, sit slightly above it, and then flatten — because the definition itself is tied only to humans. His corollary: metacognition has barely progressed because we haven't even allowed AI to think.

44:08 Two days beat everyone's two years of tuning
Recursive ran its system on three tasks: Karpathy's NanoChat (where hundreds or thousands of people using agents plus humans pushed bits per byte down to 0.937), and their system beat that in under two days; NanoGPT likewise; plus SOL-ExecBench for the Nvidia ecosystem. Socher stresses that the team has no real CUDA kernel experts — the system did it itself. Another counterintuitive finding: starting from a human seed given by an expert like Andrej produced a better final result than starting from a naive transformer — the starting point still matters.

1:02:10 Optimizing the game first means finding 30 harness bugs
While optimizing OverGrid, they found 30 bugs in the harness, which invalidated all prior research results built on those bugs, because those results were contaminated. Socher offers symmetry as a very practical check: change something that should not affect the result, and if the result changes, that's a bug. The same phenomenon shows up on multiple-choice benchmarks like GPQA — shuffle the order of A, B, and C, and the answer should not change, but the model's answer does.

item.content:encoded:
The witch hunts of the 1640s were not the embers of the Middle Ages but something lit jointly by civil war, economic collapse and religious fear: most of the accused were poor women, and the witchfinders turned that fear into a business by charging for their services.

Medium information density, but it lays out the concrete mechanics of the witch hunts: interrogation methods, the fee model, and how it crossed the Atlantic to Salem.

0:00 The witchfinder recorded his victims as a joke
The starting point for Marion Gibson's book was finding the name of the baker Meggs in the account left by the witchfinder Matthew Hopkins. Hopkins wrote in a contemptuous tone that the man had come voluntarily to be tested for witchcraft, so they hanged him — and mocked him for it. Gibson calls this ‘a terrible way to be remembered’, and so she decided to find out who the real Meggs was (actually named Henry Maggs), to tell his story with dignity and respect, and to give him back his voice. She does the same thing throughout the book: starting from the perspective of the victims of the 1640s English witch trials, rather than adopting the sneering tone of the witchfinders.

0:00 The Civil War turned England into a breeding ground for witch hunts
Gibson describes the setting: the Civil War was at its height, and England was tearing itself apart. Not just on the battlefield, but through economic dislocation and refugees on the move, many of them needing immediate relief. People were anxious, miserable and afraid, and all of those emotions fed into witchcraft accusations. At the same time, England was a deeply religious and also deeply magical society, in which people believed firmly that angels and devils existed, and were used to thinking in binary terms: if you were not on God's side, you were on the devil's. This belief system made people predisposed to believe that a witch might be living right next door.

0:00 The first case: soldiers saw a woman floating on the water
As witch hunting heated up in the 1640s, one of the earliest cases took place in 1643 on a Civil War battlefield at Newbury in Berkshire. A group of soldiers foraging after a march saw a woman floating on a plank on a nearby river and thought: ‘She is walking on water — she must be a witch.’ They dragged her before their commander, and after interrogation he ordered her shot dead. Gibson says that after that, interest in witchcraft swept across England.

0:00 They confessed not because they were guilty but because torture broke them
Many of the accused confessed. Gibson explains that besides the physical search itself being an invasive and terrifying process, these people were also deprived of sleep and made to keep their balance on a stool for hours on end while being questioned. She says these sound like torture methods, and they destroyed people's resistance. The social context played a part too: amid war and fear, local church ministers preached that the English must have sinned to bring such suffering upon themselves, that they had to repent and be vigilant against the devil. Some of the accused may genuinely have used magic, perhaps healing rituals, but either way they tended to agree with the interrogating minister or magistrate, saying: ‘All right, yes, I suppose I am indeed a witch.’

0:00 Hopkins and Stearne were self-appointed moral police
In 1645 witch hunting truly erupted in Essex. A young man from Manningtree, Matthew Hopkins, and his somewhat older friend John Stearne began to suspect there were witches nearby. Hopkins was the son of a Suffolk minister; the family seems to have been afflicted by illness, and his brother died very young, possibly of tuberculosis. Hopkins had a burning conviction that his destiny was to be a witchfinder. Stearne was also from Suffolk, married with a family, in many ways more conventional and seemingly more stable, but he too was excited by the idea that there were witches in the community. Neither man held official office, neither was recognised by the government; they were self-appointed moral police. Hopkins gave himself the title ‘Witchfinder General’.

0:00 About three-quarters of the accused were women
Looking at the history of European witch trials from the 15th to the 18th century, about 75% of the accused in known cases were women. Gibson argues this seems to be because women were more readily associated with the devil, perhaps because Eve committed the first sin in the Bible. In the 1640s society was under enormous strain, people reached for old beliefs, convinced that Satan must be the root of their problems, and so they went looking for the devil's followers. At the time almost everything was run by men, which made women vulnerable. In some towns, such as Framlingham in Suffolk, 100% of the accused were women. Many of the accused were also poor, not well educated, and had no influence in society.

0:00 The witchfinders charged for their services, until communities started counting the cost
The large-scale witch trials in the east and the Midlands gradually subsided by the end of 1647, partly because people began to question the number of the accused. In his 1648 account, Stearne wrote that he had been responsible for putting to death around 200 people — an astonishing figure. If you count everyone who was accused, interrogated or prosecuted but not executed, it runs into hundreds and hundreds. Those who were not as convinced as Stearne and Hopkins that the world was full of witches began to ask: were all these people really witches? Could England possibly have that many? Doubts about the witchfinders' motives also surfaced, especially Hopkins and Stearne, who charged for their services: they demanded lodging at inns, money to feed their horses and keep themselves, and funds to hire people to search for witch marks. The costs to the community kept piling up, and people looking at their tax bills began to think: perhaps witch trials are not a good investment.

0:00 The witch-hunting legacy crossed the Atlantic to Salem
The most famous are the Salem witch trials in Massachusetts in 1692 and 1693, where about 30 people were found guilty, 19 were hanged, and others died under torture or in prison. Events in England and Scotland had an influence more than 3,000 miles away. This was because colonists in the New World — many of them Puritans seeking religious freedom — came from the very English communities that had held witch trials earlier in the century. There are concrete examples showing that people from Framlingham and Great Yarmouth carried the idea that ‘the world is full of witches who need to be hunted’ to New England. Connecticut and Virginia also held witch trials, where settlers or their descendants remembered witch stories heard from Suffolk, Essex, Northamptonshire, Newcastle or Cornwall.
